Writing code got faster. The work around it didn’t. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment.

This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan.

What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable plan, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped issues, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.

After spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.

That review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.

Smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.

Your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard shows intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.

Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.

Figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up issues, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next plan starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.

Take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?

You don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count says you are.

We covered this topic live at GitHub Universe 2026 in “Agentic Engineering: Past the Pilot.”

#10031. Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware

In today's how-could-things-get-worse-for-Microsoft news, it seems someone's GitHub org admin creds have been compromised

Microsoft’s official agent framework package hosted on PyPI has been hijacked and now installs info-stealing malware, multiple security research firms have discovered.

CEO Satya Nadella may be on stage trying to wow investors and customers at his company’s annual Ignite conference, but somewhere in the bowels of a building in Redmond his open source team is likely panicking at what appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft’s Github organization.

The problem package is Microsoft’s agent-framework, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, researchers reported late yesterday and this morning. According to OX Security, version 1.26.1 was reverted to a safe version, but the attacker later uploaded 1.26.2 through Microsoft’s official PyPI publisher account, suggesting that, at least at the time of their report, the credentials hadn’t been locked down.

Safe to say, but if you find either version in your environment assume you have some account security work to do.

Microsoft agent-framework for Python boasts nearly 200,000 downloads a month and is used to build and deploy AI agents. As of those latest releases, it’s also being used to exfiltrate environment variables, credential files, and other secrets for Azure, Git, Docker, Hugging Face, and other sensitive developer services.

To make matters worse, the package never needs to be imported to do its dirty work – all it takes is a Python interpreter with the package installed to start up – the infected package still pulls the genuine 1.26.0 version of Microsoft’s agent-framework in order to keep itself running and looking legitimate, while in the background it gathers up credentials, encrypts them as a base64-encoded chunk of JSON, and sends them off to a webhook.site address hard coded into the malware.

It appears from researcher accounts that this is made to act fast, as the malware isn’t persistent and only runs as long as the malicious version of the agent-framework remains in a site-packages directory. What it does do, however, is not just look for credentials in the environment: It actually starts calling for new ones and collecting them, too.

In particular, the malware requests fresh identity tokens from GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, and Azure itself, which are exfiltrated to the same webhook site.

“That combination of passive theft and active token requests makes it especially dangerous in cloud build environments, because even short-lived tokens are useful when they're exfiltrated right away,” said researchers at OpenSourceMalware.

The agent-framework GitHub repo is offline as of writing. It’s been pointed out online that Microsoft’s repo for ONNX Runtime, an AI accelerator, is also offline. Other Microsoft repos remain available, and neither Microsoft nor security researchers have linked the ONNX repo’s pull to the malware campaign.

“We have made some repositories private while we investigate malicious content,” a Microsoft spokesperson told The Register. “Our priority is to protect customers and the broader ecosystem. We are working to review and will take further action as needed.”®

Updated at 1805 with comment from Microsoft.

#10030. Actual curl rewrites in rust

For a long time we have received repeated requests for, or questions about, a curl rewrite in rust. Often as a joke, but also seriously.

In this modern world of AIs, we have only been waiting for someone to prove it possible and now it seems we don’t have to wait anymore.

This fall seems to be the time of the curl-in-rust takes as we first saw urlx appear a few months ago, claimed to be a memory-safe, from-scratch reimplementation of curl and libcurl and now in November curl, rewritten in Rust – a rewrite of curl and libcurl in Rust. This second one confusingly enough not even using a different name.

This latter one claims to have spent 8,600 USD to make it happen.

Writing code once was never the big deal with software and it still isn’t. Sure, it’s fascinating that you can make a set of agents accomplish this in only a few weeks but let’s face it: it could do this because all the AIs of the world have trained on curl code for years. curl is extremely well documented, there are hundreds of existing open source application using its API and there are thousands of test cases to verify the implementation.

The C code sits there and all the AI needs to do is convert it to rust, then polish until the tests work.

curl has come to be what it is thanks to many decisions, lots of time, many users, oceans of feedback and many iterations. Sure, recreating what curl is at any specific single moment in time is certainly doable. Doable, because we have made a perfect specification for that project.

During the time these agents converted 185,000 lines of C code into 340,000 lines of Rust code (I counted), we merged over 300 commits in the actual curl project. We actually improved curl during these a little more than three weeks. A little over 200 bugfixes actually. 200 bugfixes that none of those rust rewrites have. We also fixed a few vulnerabilities. In another month we have done another 200 and maybe fixed a few more vulnerabilities. Will these clones keep up?

The constant tweaking, fixing, improving and extending is what makes a software project live, what makes it attractive to users and what makes it able to compete with alternatives.

That fixing, and occasional new feature, is a direct result of a working community of users, contributors and maintainers. That goes way beyond the source code or which language that is used.

A primary reason it is hard to make a competing curl alternative is because of the development speed, the development team and the community around curl. It is not because of the chosen language it is implemented in. Only curl can boast decades of ABI and API stability and prove that we know this and can do it well – over time. An alternative that pops up today might be able to do it as well, and in a few decades we will know if they could.

I know I’m repeating myself but: out of the 81 vulnerabilities we have confirmed in curl so far during 2026, 14 were the result of mistakes that most likely would have been avoided had we used a memory-safe language such as rust. That’s 17.3%.

A Rust implementation of curl would thus still have had 67 of those vulnerabilities.

I don’t believe in rewrites into any language. I believe in constant and never-ending polishing, iterating and refactoring.

I should add that I have not been in contact with any of the people behind these rewrites, and if there are two I bet there are more that I just haven’t seen yet. I only know of them because people have pasted me links to their repositories.

I don’t know what they will do with those projects going forward. Are they anything more than proof of concepts? I presume we will find out.

They can of course follow along our commits and convert them to rust on the fly if they want – we only do about 11 commits per day on average. Or maybe they ignore the bugreports or maybe they take their projects in other directions?

I wish them good luck whatever they decide!

Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery that mediocrity can pay to greatness. / Someone

I’m amused. A little puzzled. Fascinated. They spent their money and effort on that?

I find it quite interesting. I couldn’t possibly be part of the “just rewrite it in Rust” crowd, but I also do see the benefits in many cases.

It feels like, while ideally it’d be good to have that effort put into curl itself and see things improved and fixed, the fact that it’s a problem space people are paying attention to at all is a Good Thing™?. I hope something useful comes of them, just so we’ve got something interesting and novel to look at, at least. Maybe it leads to better understanding of the big wonderful world of internet transfers.

I appreciate the hubris – you’ve gotta start with blind, cocky optimism sometimes. 😛

“81 vulnerabilities we have confirmed in curl so far during 2026, 14 were the result of mistakes that most likely would have been avoided had we used a memory-safe language such as rust. That’s 17.3%.”

Nice, that sounds like very good motivation for a Rust rewrite.

Something that is always missing from these post-hoc analyses is the changes and features that were never implemented because the language’s unsafety made it too expensive and risky (“that which is seen and that which is not seen”). A strong type system allows you to be much more scrappy and fearless.

@Jesse: I disagree. What makes you “fearless” in development is A) a good architecture and B) a good test suite combined with C) good test and development tools. We have all that. We’re not holding back features because of the language. Never did.

If there’s anything, we have too many features and we do too much. But hey, that’s what curl is.

Isn’t a programming language just another development tool? We can talk about language capabilities just like any other.

Types and tests go together as a pair of tools. Types can be validated incrementally in less than a second (eg in rust-analyzer), tests take seconds, minutes, sometimes hours for feedback. Tests can show the presence but not the absence of bugs, types prove the absence of whole classes of bugs but not their presence. Tests tell you about a specific execution, types reason about all possible executions. Test can validate any behaviour while types can only exclude bugs provable in its logic.

The progress in programming languages has generally been towards stronger types, including lifetimes in Rust’s case. I don’t think its fair to say they have no advantages over tests.

@Jesse: different languages have different advantages and quirks, sure. I just meant that I don’t think the choice of language holds us back.

> Nice, that sounds like very good motivation for a Rust rewrite.

But I feel like you’ve missed the forest for the single tree. This whole post is describing the value in curl being the maintainers that are willing to put in the time. A single observation doesn’t outweigh the reality that code is (and always has been) cheap. But maintainer time and effort is the important part.

cURL is one of the greatest examples of a project, C or otherwise, done right. It’s a stalwart of computing. It’s literally everywhere. It’s probably even in my toaster too, which is kind of scary now that I think about it.

Jokes aside, you should really just ignore the people clamoring to rewrite it in Rust or Zig or whatever. I’m a huge Rust fan. I mainly program in Rust and a bit of C. This has nothing to do with rust per se and more to do with the internet being annoying.

An AI powered rewrite or even a rewrite by hand misses what actually makes cURL so good. It’s that there is a talented team of maintainers who understand the code, understand the domain, and are dedicated to writing and maintaining curl. Rewrites lose all of this for temporary benefits, or worse it doesn’t have any benefits at all. There are AI and hand rolled postgres rewrites in Rust that are “faster” but it turns out they’re buggy messes that aren’t even durable. They’re faster because they’re broken. 🙂

So, I say this as a huge Rust fan who contributes to a plethora or open source Rust projects. Please ignore the “riir” in Rust crowd. It doesn’t represent most of us.

” This latter one claims to have spent 8,600 USD to make it happen”. This is a wrong reading.

They claim that amount in estimated API cost equivalent, but based on them running out of quota they use a subscription, which is a lot less cost. Not that it changes anything you said though.

Thanks for keeping cURL going all these years. I doubt any of the clones are committed to similar maintainance quality and long term.

I really like what this post is talking about everyone can make a copy but who can maintain and keep on adding features in long term that is what makes it competing and survival of the copied software.

Everyone knows how Cloudflare made a copy of Next.js and everyone started posting about it for few weeks and it is dead or it is copying features from Next.js to keep up with the Next.js as it’s replacement

@Joonas The artifact mentions weekly limit only on 28/10, one week after the start of the rewrite, and not until the end of the experience, so it surely started with some heavy subscription, it may switched to token billing after to keep up with the work.

“If the work ran on a subscription plan, this is what it would have cost on the API, not what was billed.” So yes, for sure, it at least been partially subsidized, and once Anthropic will switch to token billed usage (like OpenAI will do next month, because money), it would certainly cost $8.6k for any clone, except if some “super agents” becomes the new hype and would burn way more tokens…

Again, “humans made computers for humans” is still a thing nowadays, and AI will not replacing communities tomorrow. It would have been interesting to see a clean C ? Rust ? C rewrite just to compare how the C could have been rewritten, just out of curiosity.

It is november 2026. You can use formal verification with Verus to get rid of other 67 logic bugs and then use it continuously to avoid bugs at all!

https://microsoftedge.github.io/edgevr/posts/From-Bug-Hunting-to-Bug-Prevention-with-Rust-and-Verus/

No other language yet provide such an ecosystem for error prevention.

This is such a wonderfully grounded perspective! It’s a great reminder that a software’s true strength lies in its community, history, and endless iterations—not just the language it’s written in. Thank you for everything you do for curl!

AI + Verus tool allows you to automatically write formal proofs on your code and get rid of rest 67 issues. Rust has single best ecosystem to get rid of bugs! Happy to help is you ever decide to try and collect metrics on quality improvement!

Similarly-shaped things used to happen at a much smaller scale on web 1.0. How many times I or my peers would share tarballs of our funny little webapps, only to be shown a few weeks later some proto-reactionary teenager trying so hard to impress his two or three followers with the website he “built” all on his lonesome in a day, and soon after that it’d be gone again in a fit of pique. Maybe these are the same people all aged up. Similarly-shaped things and all.

But even those kids would have the sense to not brag that they gambled away thousands of dollars to put a Pyongyang Hotel in the metaverse. That’s just sad.

I you don’t know Rust well, what makes you confident about the exact number of issues that Rust would have prevented? C is a barebone language, Rust brings much more to the table than memory safety only: – Sane type system, especially with sum types – Better error handling (mostly consequence of the previous point) – Trait-based polymorphism (no such abstraction in C) – RAII – Async (especially useful for curl)

Even users’ misusage can be prevented with a good set of types: make invalid states unrepresentable. BTW, we talk about Rust, but any functional language would do.

@Felix No one can know any exact number of problems curl would have had if written in another language. Not you, not I. What I do know though, and this is verifiable because all the details and data is public, is how many of the past curl vulnerabilities that were “C mistakes”. I think everything else in terms what other languages could do or not is mostly a distraction and “language religious talk”.

Git is releasing updates addressing six security vulnerabilities affecting clones, reference handling, merges, binary patches, and imports. Here is what users need to know.

Editor’s note (November 17, 2026): This post has been updated with additional CVE information and updated guidance for GitHub Enterprise Server users. Please see the release information below for the versions that include the fixes.

Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.An attacker-controlled Git server can exploit this discrepancy to replace a clone’s .git file or directory, redirecting Git to attacker-controlled configuration or hooks.For recursive clones, this can execute attacker-controlled code during the clone. For non-recursive clones, an attacker can replace the top-level .git directory with a file pointing to attacker-controlled repository metadata. The clone can then report an error and recommend running git status in the resulting directory; following that advice can execute attacker-controlled code.The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Robert Chen reported CVE-2026-111760, which was fixed by Elijah Newren and Toon Claes, with help from Johannes Schindelin and Jeff King. Luke Martin reported CVE-2026-113408, which was fixed by Toon Claes.

pwn2addr reported CVE-2026-114466, CVE-2026-114467, and CVE-2026-114469, which were fixed by Karthik Nayak. Kaartic Sivaraam implemented the fix for CVE-2026-105437 based on a patch by Jeff King, with help from Toon Claes and Christian Couder.

Elijah Newren is a Staff Software Engineer at GitHub. He is the designer and implementer of merge-ort, Git's default merge strategy since 2.34, author of git-filter-repo—the history rewriting tool the Git project officially recommends—and a driving force behind sparse-checkout.

#10028. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

Only some slashdot readers are humans, you insensitive clod! (sorry, couldn't resist)

These days, slashdot posts are probably consumed vastly more times by bots than by humans....

Nerds like words. You're just another bibliophobe.

While I applaud the sentiment, the current generation of "AI" literally *cannot* "do our thinking for us" -- it can *simulate* what we *think* thinking is, but it cannot actually think, by definition, since (among other reasons) we're unable to explain to it (or ourselves) in any precise and complete way, what thinking actually is (or even is not) for us. It also can't truly create anything. It can only reorganize and distill the thinking that went into what humans have already written, drawn or photographed, that make up the its training data. It may prove useful in finding things people have thought up, that we've simply missed as being important, or that we thought were wrong at the time, but none of that is "thinking" -- it's association, which is an aspect of thinking, for sure, but not the whole thing.

Ultimately AI will have no effect on "what it means to be human". It can't, since it isn't, and won't ever be anything like us. If people are thinking that it will have such an effect, they're completely deluded, which admittedly is a common malady.

The only sense in which "AI" is "changing how we talk about being human" is just that: talk. It can't change how we *are* human, or how we do things as humans. If it's changing how we talk about being human (I remain unconvinced of that fact) then possibly that's a good thing, since our understanding about "what it means to be human" and other similar philosophical questions are important, and (IMHO) in all of modern history, those kinds of questions have been insufficiently valued and explored.

It's not going to help us *answer* any of those questions, except to regurgitate, combine and reframe the kinds of answers that philosophers have already come up with over the centuries, though the answers aren't really even all that important: it's the ability to form the questions in the first place that's important and understand how the possible answers to our own questions make us feel and decide what that means for us, individually and collectively. Even if AGI someday in the far-distant future becomes a thing, it won't be able to do that "for us" and if it's truly intelligent, that's what it'll say: "The only way for you to answer that is by answering it for yourself."

Shouldn't we start at zero, though? Jan 1 isn't 1 year after December 31st.

#10026. California tells Waymo to take the next exit after freeway mishaps

Robotaxi operator suspends driverless rides on high-speed roads nationwide after construction zone incursions and a run-in with patrol vehicles

Waymo has suspended driverless freeway rides across the US after California regulators intervened over robotaxis entering construction zones and trying to bypass highway patrol vehicles.

California's DMV banned Waymo from offering driverless trips on its freeways on Wednesday, November 11. The same day, Waymo pulled the handbrake on its freeway services countrywide.

The move affects all areas in which Waymo operates on freeways, including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, and Austin. The Alphabet-owned company has not indicated how long the suspension will last. Waymo says freeway testing will continue with trained specialists behind the wheel.

Jonathan Groveman, spokesperson for the California DMV, told the Associated Press that the organization imposed the ban following two incidents involving Waymo's robotaxis that posed an "imminent hazard to public safety."

On November 5, three of the company's driverless cars entered an active construction zone on US 101 near Burlingame, south of San Francisco.

The second incident occurred the following day, and in footage shared widely online, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to drive around highway patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break – a maneuver used to slow or stop traffic.

"The Department determined that Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present," Groveman said in the statement.

Groveman said the DMV had already imposed restrictions and required corrective action following similar incidents on May 18.

Waymo subsequently recalled nearly 4,000 cars after some were caught ignoring road closure signs and cones designating construction zones in Phoenix and San Francisco.

A separate recall covered software affecting nearly 3,800 robotaxis over problems including slowing on high-speed roadways and driving into floodwater.

A Waymo spokesperson said that despite California's temporary ban, its robotaxis continue to operate on city streets across the US.

"Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," they said. "Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state.

"In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week.

"We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations."

Other nuisances and hazards caused by errant Waymos include clogging traffic in thick fog, driving into telephone poles, and killing cats and dogs. ®

Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them.

How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline.

An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database.

I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills”.

A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent, we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose:

At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification.

The When to Verify section in Proof Agent’s SKILL.md says when to invoke the skill. The remaining instructions explain what the verifier reviews and what evidence to include in its findings.

When the judgment that makes a data pipeline correct lives in four different people’s heads, those four people are the roadmap. Each change to the pipeline depends on their availability and knowledge of the data. Data Forge is an example of how to capture parts of that judgment in skills that work together.

In the support-desk pipeline example, we start with a request for metrics that count incidents created and resolved. Before building the pipeline, the forge-init skill discovers details such as source tables and naming conventions, then writes them to a resolved manifest. The other skills read that manifest for the project context they need.

The forge-builder skill then coordinates the work from the issue through to a pull request. It uses forge-dbx to query the data platform and forge-lint to apply the team’s standards as it designs and builds the pipeline. A person reviews the proposed decisions along the way, and the resulting pull request contains the pipeline code, schema changes, and tests.

Each skill has a defined responsibility, and they share project context instead of rediscovering it independently. When a step changes, you can change one skill and leave the rest alone.

Skills fit bounded, repeatable work that benefits from reusable judgment, such as a checklist, release, migration, or metric pipeline. If a workflow needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control, or permissions enforced outside the model, an application is a better fit.

We don’t want to hardcode every project’s names, database, or conventions into the skills. In the Data Forge support-desk example, a manifest describes the project, metric store, and platform so the skills can use the right project details without baking them into their instructions:

With the discovered details in the resolved manifest, the other skills don’t have to make their own assumptions about the project.

Keep discovered project details separate from team standards. The forge-init initialization skill can inspect existing schemas and code patterns; the forge-lint skill supplies the rules to follow before code is generated. A pattern found in a repository isn’t automatically a rule to preserve, so make discovered details reviewable and let people confirm or change them where business judgment is needed. To check portability, ask: could another team use these skills with its own manifest without rewriting them?

The forge-dbx skill gives the other Data Forge skills one way to access the data platform. It reads the manifest and selects a Databricks or DuckDB adapter, so each skill doesn’t need its own connection and query logic.

The manifest can choose DuckDB for the local support-desk demo, but it can’t install the DuckDB CLI or grant database access. Those remain setup responsibilities for the environment and its user. The manifest picks the engine; the host provides the access.

The Data Forge support-desk workflow has seven phases, with a human checkpoint at each one. The workflow overview shows how the skills fit together. Before a phase proceeds, the workflow checks that the previous phase is complete; before schema changes run, it asks for approval.

The Proof Agent example applies the same principle to code review. A GitHub Actions workflow gives the verifier the original request and code changes, but not the coding agent’s own assessment. The verifier returns PASS, FAIL, or PARTIAL and must cite evidence in the changed files. The GitHub Action does a static review of the diff; it doesn’t execute code or run tests. In the demo workflow, we set block-on-fail: false so findings were advisory. By default, a FAIL fails the check, which blocks the merge if the check is required. The aim is to keep test results and merge requirements in your repository’s CI checks and rules.

Supporting multiple clients can mean keeping several copies of the same instructions in sync. In the Data Forge example, we keep skills/*/SKILL.md as the source and use a packaging script to generate client-specific files: .claude-plugin/plugin.json for Claude Code, .cursor-plugin/plugin.json for Cursor, and .github/agents/*.agent.md for GitHub Copilot. The script also includes a check mode for CI:

Clients can differ in their available models, tools, credentials, and permissions. After installing a skill, check that the client recognizes it for the intended task, loads its references, can use the required tools, and returns the evidence the skill calls for.

Start with the task you’re tired of explaining. Write down what it needs, where it stops, and what a reviewer sees. Then try it with another agent and improve it as you learn what works.

#10024. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

#10022. To rank the world's biggest supercomputers, we're gonna need a bigger bench

AI has birthed some truly colossal supers, they just aren't on the Top500

For decades, the Top500 list has tirelessly ranked the world’s biggest, most powerful, and often most unique publicly-known supercomputers.

With the rise of generative AI, the list no longer lives up to its name. China’s Lineshine supercomputer at 2.2 exaFLOPS of double precision compute in the High-Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark may be the top system on the bi-annual ranking, but it’s nowhere near the biggest compute cluster in the world.

Superclusters like SpaceXAI’s Colossus, Meta’s Promethius, and OpenAI’s Stargate pack hundreds of thousands of GPUs, dwarfing anything on the Top500 today.

“These [companies] are not interested in submitting to the Top500,” Eth Zürich’s Torsten Hoefler said during his Supercomputing address this week.

It’s a dilemma that the founders of the Top500 ranking are now grappling with.  And some believe it may be time for a rethink.

“What’s really needed for tracking that more appropriately is not just a different benchmark but also different methodology,” Top500 author Erich Strohmaier said.

For a long time, Strohmaier explains, compute capability was roughly aligned with capacity.

What happened in the last few years with AI is “capacity really pulled ahead of capability in terms of market size,” he said. “We were and we still are very focused on capability.”

By capability, Strohmaier is referring to the ability to run one code across the entire cluster.

“Our prime rule for benchmarking is, you have to benchmark your whole system with one code and you cannot just add two parts up to make up a number,” he explained.

This is problematic for the large clusters major hyperscalers and cloud providers are now building to fuel the AI boom. “All those systems are capacity systems,” Strohmaier said.

In the age of AI, the top spot on the bi-annual ranking is whoever willing to run HPL instead of LLMs

They’re not designed to run one piece of code but have instead been architected to run many, many smaller or medium-sized code instantiations, which may include training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and of course inference.

Because of this, Strohmaier says, it wouldn’t be reasonable to expect SpaceXAI to run something High-Performance Linpack (HPL) on a cluster like Colossus.

But these clusters are still worth tracking. They'll just need a new benchmark better suited to judging the capability of these arrays while at the same time preventing operators from gaming the system.

What shape or form such a benchmark might take remains to be seen. Developing a new benchmark or methodology is no small task, and changing the existing benchmarks isn’t ideal. ”If we do anything to the benchmark itself, we’re going to lose the historic trends, which is extremely valuable,” Hoefler said.

Allowing for lower precisions — HPL-MxP already does this to some extent — is one avenue for addressing the fact that these accelerators are increasingly trading FP64 performance for lower-accuracy floating-point data types like FP8 or FP4.

Another avenue is developing a separate AI benchmark. This would be immediately applicable to these clusters, but with the pace of change in model architecture, building such a benchmark is challenging.

“The AI workloads change every two weeks, so if you pick something today, it’s going to be irrelevant in at most a year, and these benchmarks need to live for multiple decades,” Hoefler said. ®

In October, we experienced eight incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services.

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, new connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the issue.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

Copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Issues, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

The pool was already running near capacity when some update requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

#10020. sysdeck: Raycast for Linux & BSD

Introducing sysdeck, a command center for Linux and the BSDs that searches applications, files, the clipboard history and more from a single hotkey, and that only runs when you call it.

In August I started working on a tool that I had been missing on my Linux desktop for a while, and for which I tried to build a somewhat glued-together mess of scripts that used bemenu to do what I wanted. At some point, though, I figured that I should probably try to put together an actual program, ideally using Zig and GTK.

I wanted something that, just like bemenu (or rofi, or wofi, or whatnot), is basically a single popup that I can open with a hotkey and type a few letters into, to start an application, find a file, paste something I copied an hour ago, or convert a currency without opening a browser. Now, roughly three months later, I think I got it to a point where it’s worth publishing for others to try. It’s called sysdeck, and the way I describe it is the less bloated Linux/BSD equivalent of Raycast on macOS.

Yes, I’m aware that the title of this post is clickbait. sysdeck isn’t a port of Raycast, it doesn’t share a single line of code with it, and it doesn’t come with an extension store or a subscription plan. However, Raycast is the name that probably most people know for this kind of tool, and considering that you’re here, reading this post, the title has obviously done its job. :-)

sysdeck is supposed to be bound to a hotkey in your window manager. When you press it, a window appears in which you start typing, and sysdeck shows the matching entries from your applications, command-line executables, files and folders, browser bookmarks, clipboard history, open Sway windows, SSH hosts, Podman containers, text snippets and emoji. Return acts on the selected entry depending on its kind, meaning it launches an application, opens a file or copies a clipboard entry back. Holding Alt opens a context menu with further actions. Selected images are shown along with their EXIF data, and executables show their manual page underneath the list unless the man extension is disabled in the config.

Besides searching, sysdeck calculates and converts units and currencies using the library behind whats. It also controls running media players via MPRIS, connects and disconnects NetworkManager connections, and takes screenshots of a region, a window or the whole screen. If you configure a Gemini, OpenAI or Anthropic model, or any OpenAI-compatible server, it also sends your questions to an LLM. It keeps track of what you pick and ranks its suggestions accordingly so that it can show you recommendations that matter to your personal workflow.

Oh, and its --dmenu mode can replace dmenu in scripts, just like a single line in your Sway configuration lets it replace clipboard managers like cliphist.

What I’d like sysdeck to become is the one command center from which you start, find and control everything on a Linux or BSD desktop, instead of the collection of single-purpose tools and scripts that a typical tiling window manager setup combines for launching programs, managing the clipboard, picking emoji and taking screenshots. As mentioned before, sysdeck is written in Zig, uses GTK4 for its interface and keeps its indexes in SQLite.

One part of sysdeck’s design that differs from most launchers that come with more advanced features is that sysdeck doesn’t use a background service. This is deliberate and will stay that way for the foreseeable future.

Raycast, for example, keeps running at all times, so that its window can appear the instant you press the hotkey. sysdeck, however, only runs when you ask for it. Every press of the hotkey starts a new process that shows the window, does what you asked it to do, and exits as soon as you pick an entry, press Escape or switch to another window. Whenever one of its indexes is older than its configured maximum age, sysdeck rebuilds it on a separate thread while the window is open, and searches the existing index in the meantime.

Similarly, even the clipboard history works without a resident process of its own, because wl-paste starts a lightweight sysdeck process (that only loads the absolute necessary bits) for every copy. That run records the entry and exits again, all within 10 to 20 milliseconds. The price for all of this is a start time of about a tenth of a second on my machine, most of which GTK spends on building and presenting the window. In my opinion this “slight delay” is a fair trade over running a background service, because RAM has become expensive and hard to get, as I’ve outlined in my posts on holding on to your hardware and on dealing with faulty RAM, and I believe that a program that is on screen for only a few seconds at a time shouldn’t occupy memory and eat up CPU cycles for the rest of the day.

sysdeck uses the whats library for conversions and can convert various units and currencies.

You can configure custom web search engines and search them directly from sysdeck, which then opens your default browser with the results.

sysdeck can be configured to index specific folders and include their contents in its search results. In disk mode it shows only those items.

Using MPRIS, sysdeck can control media players and trigger actions such as play, pause, skip the current track or go back to the previous one, and it can also show what is currently playing from within its UI.

sysdeck builds an index of all available emoji and lets you search for individual ones using keywords that make sense, so that you find the one you’re looking for, which it then copies to your clipboard on Return.

Podman containers can be started and stopped from within sysdeck, which also shows the current status of each individual container.

Anyway, sysdeck is open source under the SEGV License and its primary repository is on tty.fail, with a mirror on GitHub that also publishes pre-built binaries. The latest release includes builds for Linux on x86_64, aarch64, riscv64, powerpc64le and s390x, each for glibc as well as musl, a musl build for loongarch64, and x86_64 builds for FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD. The binaries use your system’s GTK4 libraries. If you’d rather build sysdeck yourself, the README lists the packages you need on each of these systems.

If a keyboard-driven command center that only runs when you need it sounds like your kind of thing, give sysdeck a try, and let me know how it works for you in the community channel.

Enjoyed this? Please consider supporting my work.
