#9989. Security advisories: multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion

Seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution. We have released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix them. We strongly recommend upgrading.

CVE identifiers have been requested for these vulnerabilities but have not been assigned yet, so this advisory refers to them by their GitHub Security Advisory (GHSA) identifiers.

Ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

Ruby has a double free in its regular expression engine. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

Ruby has an integer overflow in the case conversion of strings, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching against a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that use attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can lead to memory corruption in an attacker-controlled way.

Ruby has an integer overflow in its regular expression engine, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

Ruby has a heap-based buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s. Converting a crafted regular expression to a string may allow information disclosure or remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching a crafted string may disclose memory contents or crash the process.

We strongly recommend upgrading to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14.

Ruby 3.3 is in the security maintenance phase. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached their end of life and will not receive these fixes.

#9988. US Government Email Systems Open to Abuse Thanks to Typos

Erroneous or outdated DNS records can give attackers surprising powers over organizations' email systems.

Simple oversights in domain name system (DNS) records are exposing government organizations to all kinds of potential impersonation, spying, and more.

In a new study of more than 25,000 government-related domains, SH Consulting founder Alex Shakhov found dozens whose DNS records referenced either mistyped, expired, or otherwise repurposed domains. Though few in number, those vulnerable included all sorts of agencies representing US towns, cities, counties, regulatory boards, and more.

Many of the erroneous records pointed to domains that were either available to, or already snapped up by, attackers. Depending on the nature of the error, they could allow attackers to send or receive email on behalf of vulnerable government agencies, reconfigure their DNS records, read their security records, and more.

"Typos in DNS are very dangerous, because technically the organization is being hacked without anyone breaking into its systems," Shakhov tells Dark Reading. "You already have a domain with a reputation established over years. You put whatever IPs you want into DNS, spin up an email server, and send emails out, exploiting that reputation and users' trust. And these attacks are very difficult to detect, because the attackers didn't break anything. They just registered a domain sitting in the DNS that nobody knew existed."

Related:As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up

After Dark Reading ran this story, Livingston County, Mich., the city of Waynesboro, Tenn., and the Alabama legislature have all implemented or begun working on fixes for their DNS vulnerabilities.

Little matters more to a website's security than its DNS records, which include instructions about where the website lives in IP space (A/AAAA), its domain (CNAME), how its email is handled (MX, TXT), and who decides these details in the first place (NS). At the end of the day, though, it's a totally public set of information in plaintext. A simple typo in any of these instructions can have surprisingly significant impacts.

Take Livingston County, Mich., and the city of Pikeville, Ky. These two government bodies seem to have authorized Amazon's Simple Email Service (SES) for its day-to-day email needs and, as such, their TXT records specify it as a trusted third-party provider. The domains they list, however, contain typos: "amzonses[.]com" and "amasonses[.]com." Thanks to these mistakes, these bodies have been allowing a non-Amazon entity to send emails on their behalf.

To what end? When Shakhov checked the two organizations' Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allowlists, he found that Pikeville's listed 75 IP addresses, and Livingston's listed more than 32,000 different IP addresses, all authorized to send mail on behalf of their official domains. As a result, Pikeville's official government domain is now listed on the URI blacklist website "URIBL," and Shakhov assessed that "it's reasonable to assume the domain is still being used for abuse."

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

In the Livingston County case, the "included" SPF list was rotated every three to eight days since 2021. This suggested that an attacker was performing a "snowshoe" operation: switching to new sending IPs, sending unwanted or malicious emails, and once those IPs attained bad reputations, cycling in new ones.

This information alone doesn't necessarily prove that attackers were abusing Livingston County's email domain, or prove how much they might have. But it does prove that they could have. Shakhov connected the actor behind this compromise to a previously documented group that was seen abusing websites from major corporations such as Oracle and CNN Money as well as universities — like the Universities of California in Los Angeles, Davis, San Diego, and Santa Cruz (UCLA, UC Davis, UC San Diego, and UC Santa Cruz) — and the Connecticut state government, thanks to expired CNAME records.

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

Just about any DNS record can be abused if it contains a typo or refers to an otherwise incorrect domain for some other reason. The nature of the abuse depends, however, on the record in question. Once they register a so-called "dangling" (purchasable) domain, attackers can intercept mail (if the issue lies with an MX record), serve spam content (if it's in CNAME or NS), send phishing that appears to come from a legitimate sender (SPF), or collect security intel through Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC).

For example, the website for the City of Rupert, Idaho, currently refers to its neighbor Heyburn's old domain name, heyburnidaho[.]org. That domain was purchased by a malicious actor, which reworked its name server (NS) records to point to its shady gambling website. The actor also arranged to be able to send and receive emails from addresses with an @heyburnidaho.org suffix.

A less serious exposure could occur if attackers grab hold of a DMARC reporting domain. DMARC is an email security protocol, and its part of a TXT record can tell a mail server where to send reports. Those reports can contain sensitive information about an organization's email infrastructure. Shakhov found 11 local government institutions at risk of this sort of information theft, including four county and law enforcement agencies from Jennings County, Ind.

Taking advantage of these situations is one of the easiest jobs hackers can choose for themselves. "Attackers constantly scan DNS records for vulnerabilities and mistyped domains, because it's one of the easiest and cheapest ways to get into someone's infrastructure," Shakhov explains.

"Records at the root domain, like MX, NS, SPF, DMARC, CAA, etc., can be looked up by anyone," he continues. "Subdomains are harder to find, but Certificate Transparency logs reveal most of them. So attackers just scan DNS in bulk and get whatever they want. It's even easier for government domains, because it’s only about 26,000 domains to scan, and attackers can do it multiple times a day at almost no cost. CISA even publishes the full list of .gov domains, so attackers don't have to find them."

Shakhov laments that while DNS has been around for nearly half a century, "There's typically no one at an organization responsible for DNS management. As a result, over time it often turns into a graveyard of expired domains from previous vendors, former corporate domains forgotten after acquisitions and mergers, or just typos, when someone typed a record by hand instead of copying and pasting it."

Proper DNS hygiene, he says, requires that organizations follow at least a few core processes. First of all, he argues, "Admins and IT teams must stop typing DNS records by hand. Across millions of domains we scanned this year, 47% of the unregistered domains we found in SPF and DMARC records were typos, either of the organization's own domain or of a provider's."

Second, organizations must have a map of their DNS infrastructure and know where every DNS record came from. Depending on the circumstances, this can be easier said than done. "At universities, it's quite common for students to put a project on GitHub and ask the IT team to add a CNAME so it lives under the university domain," Shakhov explains. "The student graduates, but the CNAME stays. The GitHub account gets abandoned and removed, so whoever creates an account with the same name already has a CNAME sitting under the university's DNS."

Organizations should also consider registering misspelled versions of their own domains to prevent attackers from snapping them up later.

And, finally, "Regular DNS audits are a must," Shakhov says. "In most cases, it's just a simple script that scans your DNS for invalid domains or destinations and flags them. It's never been that difficult to do a quarterly DNS review to make sure everything is up to date."

This story was updated at 3:05 p.m. ET on Nov. 10 to reflect actions by multiple US government agencies to address their DNS vulnerabilities.

Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9987. Announcing XRAID: declustered parity RAID for zoned XFS

Christoph Hellwig has announced the initial public release of XRAID—declustered parity RAID that is integrated into XFS.

The two primary aims of XRAID are to support parity RAID on zoned devices like SMR hard drives, and to provide a fast RAID implementation without inherent data integrity problems. XRAID, just like zoned XFS also works on conventional hard drives and SSDs. Optimizing for SSD performance has not been a focus, but even without that, writes are up to 20 times faster than mdraid. [...]

Work on XRAID has been ongoing for a year and a half, and while we aren't anywhere near ready for an upstream submission, we are interested in feedback and testing from a wider audience now. The current implementation supports zero to 2 parities. We did experiments with the SnapRAID parity library to support 3 and more parities, and while that is not included in the current version, support for more parities is planned and the code is prepared for it.

The xfsprogs branch includes mkfs support and a new "xraid" utility for managing devices and inspecting an XRAID file-systems. We have also extended Zonar (The zoned file-system visualisation tool) to show how each logical zone maps onto physical zones on devices.

Hellwig gave a presentation at FOSSY in August on this topic; video of the talk does not seem to be available yet, but his slides are available.

#9986. The Magic of Partial Evaluation

There are certain ideas in software that are simply beautiful. It doesn't matter if they have any practical use. It doesn't matter that you will never convince your coworkers to consider them. There is just something captivating about the way some computational systems work.

For me, the most beautiful pieces of software are those that reveal something about the nature of programming languages. Programming languages are my obsession. I have never met a problem that couldn't be solved by introducing yet another programming language. Solving a problem at the programming language level is about solving the meta problem. Instead of trying to solve a particular problem, we take a step back and ask how we can solve a whole class of problems at once.

So when I find something that makes me rethink the nature of programming languages, I start rethinking computation as a whole. One of these incredibly beautiful but tricky concepts goes by the name partial evaluation. If you are fascinated by interpreters and compilers, partial evaluation will teach you how they are related, and how you can get a compiler for free.

Partial evaluation has been a fascination of mine for a while. But this whole thing came up when James Long announced he had revived Meta's partial evaluator for JavaScript called prepack. When I first heard about prepack, I had some high hopes and expectations for the project, but was sadly let down. This revival brought to light those same dreams. But sadly, just as with the original aim, prepack was not designed for beauty, but for practicality. So I figured it was time to renew my own efforts.

Yes, in some ways this is a post repping my own library I'm releasing. But I'm not doing this because I want it to be used. I'm doing this because it lets you play with the idea I find so beautiful. That is what this post is about.

As a person who reads code, you can think about how this code computes and what answer it will give. But you can do more than just give the answer. You can see the expanded form of this particular code for these particular calls. This code is spiritually the same as the following expression, once we expand it out.

In this case, there is really nothing at all that this code needs to do at runtime. A sufficiently smart compiler will just run this code directly at compile time and give the answer. But this is a bit less clear if things come in at runtime.

It might seem like we can't do anything here, but again, if you are used to thinking about how programs run, you can trace this out and realize this is just the same as:

What we have done in both of these cases is called partial evaluation. In the first, it was a trivial case because everything was statically known. But in this latter case, we have reduced a program down into the essentials of its dynamic structure. There are no recursive function calls left. All of this has been expanded as far as it could till we get just the dynamic parts of the code remaining.

This intuitive notion of partial evaluation is all you need to know to appreciate the beauty here. Partial evaluation just evaluates the part of the program we can evaluate at build time and leaves all the rest. When we do this with certain programs in certain combinations, we get some quite surprising, incredible behavior.

Here we have a very simple interpreter for a language that just supports arithmetic. For the above expression, you should be able to think about how we could start "partially" evaluating it. (In this case, it can be a full evaluation.) If this kind of partial evaluation isn't quite clicking for you, I've put the steps below to hopefully help it make sense.

This is a simple evaluation of the code. But what happens if we throw a value we don't know into the expression?

Here we can see that clear partial evaluation difference. We don't know how to evaluate Number(process.argv[2]). We have no idea what the answer to that will be. But as part of this process, we do know some partial information about it. For example, when we get to

we know that Number(process.argv[2]) is indeed a number. So we can partially evaluate it further. Hopefully this is all making sense. But if you are like me, this all might seem a bit trivial and uninteresting. So let's look at a more complicated example.

Here we have a brainfuck interpreter. And the example program we want to partially evaluate does not require any input at all (in brainfuck , is the way you get input). So when we go to partially evaluate this, we will just get an answer. In this case, this program is actually brainfuck's "hello world". But what about a program with input?

When we do our partial evaluation, we get the following:

What is this? A compiled brainfuck program! This is the first incredible fact: when you take an interpreter and partially evaluate it with a program, you get the compiled program out! Now this particular exact form is an artifact of how my partial evaluator works. You could imagine slightly different code. But the key is that what we've done is remove the interpreter completely.

What we've discovered here is the first of three so-called Futamura Projections. Our partial evaluator, when applied to an interpreter and given a program, can give us a compiled version of that program. Or to put it in pseudocode.

Depending on your exposure to interpreters and compilers, this might seem miraculous or mundane. Writing an interpreter and writing a compiler can seem like significantly different undertakings. In the age of AI, perhaps less so, but I think even then many things still hold. It is quite easy to instrument an interpreter, quite a bit harder to do so for a compiler. Changing an interpreter to support new features is quite easy, less so for a compiler. But more than that, there are all sorts of things that can be thought of as interpreters, that we'd almost never write a compiler for.

Consider this simple schema setup. This is code that can easily be partially evaled into something where we have created specialized functions for our particular schema. While not the most crucial code, this can give us a 5x performance boost when our objects start getting more complicated. You may think that we should just hand-write those functions. Or hand-write a compiler for these schemas. But what about those schemas that exist only at runtime? Now we either need to compile those on the fly, or we have to keep both a compiler and interpreter. Having a way to partial eval lowers this burden quite a bit.

But if the Futamura projections stopped here, they would be exciting, but not quite the craziness they are. To understand how this can go further, we are going to take this a step beyond your raw intuition of what it means to partially evaluate something and give a different frame. We can think of partial evaluation as a process of "specializing" a program.

What exactly is specializing a program? Well, it is taking a program that is generic and making a version that instead works for a single program. Let's think about a simple pattern matcher program like an overly simplified regex.

This program is generic. It lets you match on many different patterns. That can be great if we need that flexibility. But if you don't have a bunch of patterns, it might be worth it to just make specialized code. Now, exactly what kind of specialized code? It might be that you only have this literal pattern; then you want to specialize very particularly.

Or you just have *** as a pattern.

For any bit of generic code, we can think of how to move our code to a more specialized form.

Partial evaluation is a form of specialization that figures out what it should specialize on based on what input is static and what is dynamic. In many ways, a partial evaluator is a generic specializer. Given any program, we can make a specialized version of it for any input. What happens if we specialize an interpreter for a given input? We get back that interpreter for only exactly that one program. But what do we need then? Do we need all this generic dispatch? No, we know the full program. We don't need any operations we don't actually use. We can fully get rid of all the generic interpreter mechanism.

But if the specializer can specialize any program, can it specialize itself?

This leads us to the second Futamura projection. Put in our pseudo-code format, we get:

Or, to put it in our specializer language, what if we make a special version of our generic specializer? What is it specialized for? A particular interpreter. Now we have a function that, given any program, will spit out newly specialized interpreters just for that program. Or, in Java speak, we have a specialized interpreter factory.

Let's see a real example of one of these compilers to make this concrete. Here is the interpreter we are going to specialize.

When we apply our second projection, we get out the following compiler:

And if we compile one of these very simple programs, we can see the output:

Now, of course, this is not a very interesting language. But hopefully you can see this general idea. Given an interpreter, we automatically derive a compiler! Pretty incredible.

But we can't stop at the second projection. We have to push on and get to the final mind-bending projection. If you apply our specializer to itself as input, you get a compiler generator.

So now we have a generic function that will spit out compilers for any interpreter we give it!

I have implemented a reasonable, but still very limited partial evaluator for JavaScript in Rust. I have taken it further to try to make it work quite well for a number of different interpreters and interpreter-like programs in JavaScript. I've also tried to get limited versions of the second and third projections working. Go play with it, see what works, what doesn't, file issues, or better, use some of your tokens to help me make more cases work.

But most of all, explore. This is such a rich space. Below are some papers, blogs, and projects about partial evaluation in some way, shape, or form. There has never been a better time to play with these kinds of crazy techniques for programming languages. Don't let what is practical stop you from exploring the cool, interesting aspects of programming.

#9985. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9984. Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

A operação, que contou com o uso de inteligência artificial, utilizou e-mails falsos, documentos governamentais falsificados e a criação de uma organização local para atacar escolas no Peru e no Equador, entre outras ações.

This translation was generated with our internal AI tool.

Uma operação de influência sediada na Rússia enviou e-mails se passando por autoridades educacionais do Peru e do Equador, levando algumas escolas a realizar eventos que os operadores então utilizaram para alimentar controvérsias, de acordo com um relatório divulgado pela OpenAI.

A operação de “fachada falsa”, apelidada de “Dark Clark,” utilizou uma combinação de planejamento baseado em IA e relatórios, além de técnicas mais tradicionais, para convencer administradores escolares a celebrar um “Dia Nacional da Diversidade Cultural e Linguística” em 21 de maio e a destacar três figuras políticas ucranianas, que foram então usadas para tentar semear divisão, afirmou a OpenAI em uma análise do uso operacional de seus modelos de IA. Em outras campanhas, como as direcionadas à Argentina e à Bolívia, as operações russas pareciam ter como objetivo influenciar a política local.

Related:Russia's Cold Relic APT Turns One Cloud Breach Into Another

Os supostos operadores russos utilizaram IA para tornar seu fluxo de trabalho mais eficiente, redigindo relatórios internos sobre suas atividades e, em alguns casos, criando conteúdo para suas campanhas, informou a empresa.

“A IA pode conferir a essas operações de fachada maior escala, eficiência, fluência linguística e capacidade editorial”, afirmou a OpenAI em sua análise. “Os operadores podem usar essas vantagens para explorar vítimas desavisadas, como funcionários ou editores, e divulgar seu conteúdo para públicos que não têm ideia de quem está por trás disso, nem quais são suas motivações.”

A América Latina tornou-se um palco cibernético de espionagem e operações de influência na disputa entre as principais potências globais, tornando-se a região mais atacada ciberneticamente no mundo. Atores conhecidos ligados à China tiveram como alvo tanto a Venezuela quanto o Panamá no início deste ano para obter informações sobre a política na região e proteger os interesses petrolíferos do país. A Rússia expandiu suas operações de inteligência cibernética e desinformação, principalmente para frustrar os esforços dos EUA na região, de acordo com um relatório da RAND de 2026.

“A Rússia também mantém capacidades cibernéticas para realizar invasões direcionadas e desinformação com o objetivo de semear divisão política, perturbar a percepção da situação e enfraquecer as mensagens dos EUA em situações de crise”, afirmou o relatório da RAND.

A operação russa parece estar ligada a uma entidade conhecida como “Politology” ou “La Compania”, que tem vínculos com o falecido oligarca russo Yevgeniy Prigozhin, com o objetivo de influenciar a política global, de acordo com a análise da OpenAI. Os relatórios fornecidos ao modelo de IA continham informações detalhadas sobre as operações do grupo, incluindo detalhes sobre trabalhos anteriores que os ligavam aos grupos de Prigozhin.

Related:China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

O ataque de desinformação contra escolas em Lima, no Peru, foi uma das campanhas descritas pelos atacantes. Ao elaborar uma diretiva com aparência oficial para os administradores escolares, citando um fictício “Dia da Diversidade Cultural e Linguística”, eles solicitaram que os alunos participassem de atividades de 10 a 15 minutos para aprender sobre três figuras políticas ucranianas. Posteriormente, os operadores instruíram os administradores a enviar fotos do evento.

A OpenAI investigou os eventos e encontrou detalhes que corroboravam as alegações dos operadores, disse Ben Nimmo, pesquisador-chefe da equipe de inteligência e investigações da OpenAI, à Dark Reading. O Ministério da Educação do Peru emitiu uma carta oficial (em espanhol) dois meses depois, mencionando a diretiva e informando que a embaixada da Ucrânia havia identificado a fraude em sua própria carta, datada de 25 de maio.

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

“Nunca se deve acreditar em um agente de ameaças pelo que ele diz, certo?”, diz Nimmo. “ Para cada alegação, buscamos evidências na internet que a corroborassem. Para algumas das alegações que eles fizeram, simplesmente não conseguimos encontrar evidências. Talvez tenham sido removidas, talvez estivessem em lugares que não seriam encontrados por meio de uma busca em fontes abertas, talvez nunca tenham acontecido.”

Uma diretiva fraudulenta enviada às escolas de Lima, no Peru, por supostos agentes de desinformação russos. Fonte: Ministério da Educação do Peru (traduzido pelo Claude Opus 5.5)

Como a operação resultou em um político na Polônia citando os eventos, a OpenAI classificou o sucesso com nota 5 na Escala de Impacto de Operações de Influência de seis pontos.

Os operadores russos usaram técnicas semelhantes para induzir escolas no Equador a realizar uma cerimônia de juramento de lealdade ao presidente Daniel Noboa e a Erik Prince, ex-chefe da empresa militar privada Blackwater, afirmou a OpenAI em sua análise. Algumas escolas seguiram a orientação, o que levou a cobertura jornalística e uma denúncia oficial por parte do Ministro da Educação.

Os operadores alegaram ter conduzido com sucesso outras operações de influência das quais a OpenAI não conseguiu encontrar evidências, incluindo a divulgação de uma história de que uma influenciadora brasileira nas redes sociais teria sido traficada para a Ucrânia e a disseminação de um trecho de áudio que alegava que bancos bolivianos pretendiam limitar saques em dinheiro. Os operadores também, ocasionalmente, pediam ao ChatGPT para encontrar incidentes regionais pelos quais pudessem assumir o crédito, diz Nimmo.

Os operadores russos criaram uma chamada “plataforma de pesquisa”, denominada Social Research Center, que contratava funcionários regionais para criar conteúdo local, sem que eles soubessem que a organização fazia parte de uma iniciativa de desinformação.

Embora as operações tivessem como alvo a América Latina, a intenção era prejudicar as relações entre a Ucrânia e o resto do mundo, afirma Nimmo, da OpenAI.

“A maneira como eu encaro essa operação como um todo é que ela gira em torno da Ucrânia”, diz ele. “Trata-se de fazer a Ucrânia parecer mal.”

De modo geral, o uso da IA não abriu novos caminhos para ataques nem criou novas oportunidades de desinformação, mas a tecnologia fez com que as traduções para o idioma nativo soassem mais naturais, permitiu que os operadores assumissem papéis específicos com mais facilidade e simplificou o fluxo de trabalho da operação, afirma Nimmo.

“Se você pensar na Agência de Pesquisa na Internet e no inglês desleixado deles, acho que a IA realmente oferece uma vantagem incremental”, diz ele. “Mas não tenho a impressão de que o uso do nosso modelo tenha sido o fator decisivo. De certa forma, o manual de táticas era muito, muito tradicional.”

InfoQ Homepage News Uber’s Legal AI Agent Cuts Contract Review Time by 20% with Rules and RAG

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read

Uber’s Legal Redlining Agent has reduced average contract review time by more than 20%, with 91% accuracy in AI-generated decisions, according to the company. Integrated into Microsoft Word, the agent analyzes proposed contract changes, assesses legal risks, and recommends policy-aligned responses using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), historical lawyer feedback, and deterministic rules. Lawyers retain responsibility for reviewing and approving its recommendations.

The agent identifies edits proposed by external parties, interprets their intent, compares changes with legal policies, and suggests whether to accept, reject, or modify clauses. It also generates comments explaining recommendations and flags changes requiring closer scrutiny. Uber began developing the first generation in early 2024 and piloted it with its Legal team in 2025.

High-level workflow of the Legal Redlining Add-in / Agent (Source: Uber Blog Post)

An initial RAG implementation retrieved relevant sections from legal playbooks to guide language model responses. However, the system struggled with semantic retrieval accuracy, negotiation tone, and scenarios not covered by existing examples. Uber subsequently added a feedback loop that captures lawyers’ decisions, reasoning, and final edited text.

This change allowed the agent to retrieve examples of how similar clauses had been handled rather than relying only on whether a previous recommendation was accepted or rejected. At runtime, similarity search and metadata filtering narrow thousands of historical interactions to approximately 20 candidates. A second language model-based filtering stage evaluates their relevance. Exponential decay weighting, with a configurable half-life currently set to 365 days, prioritizes recent decisions while retaining older examples. The implementation also gives domain experts control over language and negotiation style.

Uber Engineering framed the challenge in its LinkedIn post:

How can AI help streamline repetitive contract review while keeping lawyers in control?

The legal team defines the desired tone and style, while engineers maintain the prompt structure and application workflow. The architecture combines a React and TypeScript Word add-in with a Python backend orchestrated through LangGraph. Parallel workflow nodes handle intent detection, risk assessment, and policy lookup. OpenSearch stores vectorized legal rules and historical feedback, while Redis maintains session state for follow-up questions.

Legal Redlining Agent system architecture (Source: Uber Blog Post)

A deterministic rules engine enforces non-negotiable legal requirements and overrides model recommendations when a matching rule applies. Language models handle tasks requiring contextual interpretation, including clause recommendations and negotiation tone. A final verification step checks generated responses against retrieved rules.

Uber is also exploring agentic harnesses, including Claude Code and OpenCode, alongside skills to structure and automate workflows across its agentic AI efforts. The team plans to investigate legal ontologies and knowledge graphs to represent legal concepts and relationships, providing a semantic foundation for more consistent interpretation and reasoning.

#9981. How I made a custom game engine for Satelital

Seven years ago I decided to start learning how to make a game from scratch. And Last week I released Satelital, a rule-discovery game about learning alien logic.

As a solo developer, I decided to start this project from scratch. My motivation was to learn the actual fundamentals behind the technology of videogames. This meant I had to build most of the tools I would need myself, including the game engine, renderer, puzzles, editors, UX, design, art and music.

Now that I've finally managed to release the game, I think it's a good moment to share how I built it.

The main reason I got into programming was the idea of eventually working on games. I spent many years working on web and building mobile apps. It was fun, but I felt like I wasn't going in the direction I really wanted to.

So one day, after listening to every Jonathan Blow talk I could find and playing too much The Witness, I decided to finally give it a try.

I spent many days and countless hours looking for the best tool I could use to make a game, but nothing left me satisfied. The closest I got to having fun with gamedev was with the LÖVE framework making a few jam games. But even with that, it felt quite limiting to not really know what was happening behind the graphics I somehow managed to animate on my screen.

I remember hearing about shaders and parallel programming. The concept always felt very arcane and mysterious to me, but now writing them is the thing I enjoy the most while coding.

I finally decided to jump into the swimming pool and actually learn C⁠+⁠+. I had to learn how to manage memory and how not to shoot myself in the foot with the wrong tools. I started using SDL2 while trying to use the C⁠+⁠+ standard library as little as possible.

Before getting too deep into the engine, I actually finished a prototype of the puzzles not long after learning how to draw some simple graphics with C⁠+⁠+. It had very early versions of four kinds of puzzles that mostly survived until the final game. It was made entirely with SDL2, but I soon realised that if I wanted more interesting graphics, I would need to use shaders and decided to switch to OpenGL.

With the help of LearnOpenGL I quickly had a triangle on the screen. From there, learning things like lighting, tonemapping, normal maps, shader effects and everything else opened up a whole new way of looking at computers for me. Before, my idea of how a computer actually draws to the screen was quite naive. When I started learning graphics I just wanted to be able to manually change the color of each pixel individually, but in the end the idea of running a program in parallel for every pixel clicked for me.

One thing that made a huge difference while working on shaders was having code reloading. Before that, I had a complex system that stored constant values in config files, which would later get passed through uniforms into shaders. Then a custom development menu would provide some UI to tweak those values at runtime. With that I stopped having to reload and compile everything for every little change I wanted to make.

It worked, but having to maintain all this extra scaffolding was slowing me down. Another unexpected downside of this setup was that, in some cases, the shader compiler couldn't optimize the code as well as it otherwise could, since knowing constant values ahead of time helps it make better decisions.

Having shader reloading made a huge difference. Being able to change some code, save the file and immediately see the result on screen was very useful. Iterating on shaders became much faster and more fun. This was probably my biggest regret about not having it from day one.

For a big part of the development I was using SDL2, mainly to create a window, read input and get a surface to draw on. But it felt wrong to depend on a library that was several times bigger than my entire game just to handle a few seemingly simple tasks. I decided to drop that dependency and make my own platform layer that I could understand and maintain. I wouldn't have to wait for someone else to fix a bug anymore because now I could just change it myself. It wasn't that hard to end up with a single file with a few thousand lines of code that supported both macOS and Windows. I'm now looking forward to working on mobile and console ports, it feels like it might be a fun thing to work on.

At some point during development, compile times were getting longer, so I decided to look into what was going on. I checked where all that time was going, and to my surprise a lot of it was spent compiling standard library things. Stuff like std::function was particularly slow for example.

Eventually I realised that I wasn't actually forced to use the standard library just because it was there, and the subset I needed wasn't that hard to implement myself. It took me a month to replace it with my own base library, but it was so worth it. Not only did compile times get faster, but I also learned how a lot of things I had always taken for granted in other languages actually worked.

At some point I started looking into Vulkan because I wanted HDR. I couldn't get it working on macOS through OpenGL and I was worried about OpenGL being deprecated in the future. Also I didn't really want to build the whole engine around an API that might become deprecated.

Moving to Vulkan was rough at the beginning. There was so much boilerplate to type and understand. Also, when I started working on the engine, there wasn't much documentation around how to implement a good backend with it. In hindsight, I feel that even though I got a lot of valuable things from tutorials and books, most of them were overcomplicating something that could be much more straightforward. I still have nightmares about trying to resize a window...

Getting Vulkan working on macOS was actually surprisingly easy thanks to MoltenVK. It was nice not having to learn Metal and being able to keep the same codebase on Windows. The engine started out only working on macOS, so I was afraid I'd run into a lot of issues when porting it to Windows. But I was quite nice to see Vulkan just working the same day I tried it.

My philosophy from day one was to only grow the engine towards exactly what I needed. This was a long solo project, so trying to build a general purpose engine first, without knowing what I needed, would probably have meant never finishing the game. I did waste time on things I thought I would need, but I cut them when I knew I wouldn't be using them. Because I was also learning C/C⁠+⁠+ along the way, I made many coding mistakes but I wasn't afraid of big refactors. Cleaning the codebase helped me bring up my morale.

From the beginning I wanted to avoid making a 3D engine since I knew that might complicate things too much. But after I finished the prototype, I kept learning about shader techniques and effects. So in the end, my goal was to get as close as possible to a 3D look without actually having to load any 3D polygons.

To do this, I chose an orthographic top-down view so I could just prerender the assets in Blender and then load their albedo, normal and height maps as textures. Having a fixed camera meant I could render all the assets from exactly the same perspective, so they would always fit together properly in the game. Other things that needed to be animated were drawn in the pixel shader using SDFs. The terrain of the planets was too big to be stored entirely in textures, so in most cases I had to procedurally generate them in shaders too.

Since I wanted a 3D look with dynamic lighting, I also needed dynamic shadows. The final approach I settled on was ray marching. With the height map of each prop, I could make them look as if they were actually sitting in a 3D space, even though everything was still rendered in 2D. In the shader I basically march along the direction of the light and sample the height map to figure out where a shadow should be drawn.

Having the height map was also useful for other things. For example, I could use that information to make objects interact with the water in a convincing way. Objects can actually submerge in the ocean instead of looking like flat images drawn on top of it. This is also how the waves can interact with the shore around an island.

The engine was only one part of making a complete game. I also had to build a custom level editor. I wanted to make it as easy as possible to design and iterate on puzzles, so I integrated an edit mode that allowed me to change puzzles and the enviroment at runtime and see the changes in real time.

It was quite fun to quickly draw and tweak puzzles directly in the game. It helped me discover so many ideas. After making thousands of puzzles, you start to develop a sense of beauty about how a puzzle should be. Having this editor allowed me to get into the zone. I could spend hours making puzzles without actually thinking about the tool I was using.

Alongside the in-game editor I made a custom Blender plugin that could load my level config files into Blender. The game had a file watcher that could detect changes in the baked textures of the 3D models rendered by Blender. But it could also load level data and provide another way to edit. The upside was being able to just use Blender tools like multi-select, but aside from that, it wasn't actually that useful. It was cool to make though, and it's an interesting demo. But just being able to edit things in-game was much better, since you can see how it will actually look in the end. Though having said that, looking at the levels in an actual 3D environment feels quite nice.

Building the game with all these custom tools brought some issues. They worked on my machine, but when I started playtesting I began to find lots of bugs that were tricky to reproduce. The hardest ones were related to graphics, due to differences in hardware and drivers on machines I didn't have access to. Tools like Vulkan validation layers were quite useful, though they didn't catch everything.

Another thing that was tricky to deal with was shader compatibility. When using GLSL, if you rely heavily on making visual effects with noise related functions, you will find issues with things like sin or pow because the specification doesn't guarantee their precision. So I had to be constantly checking that everything looked the same on as many different hardware configurations as I could find. For a while, I didn't notice that the distribution pattern of my stars looked different across vendors. It looked correct, but I wanted to have the same placement of stars wherever you played to make it feel more like an actual place.

Having good logs to see how the internals of the game were working ended up being very useful. It was essential for me to have them after I released the demo and started getting feedback from users who were seeing errors I couldn't reproduce. Many of them reported a black screen when trying to open the game for the first time, and these were caused by many different kinds of problems. Sometimes it would be a missing extension, sometimes a third party Vulkan layer injecting code that prevented the frame from being drawn, or some other particular driver issue. Without the logs showing the exact point when the error happened, it would have been almost impossible to fix these bugs without having the actual hardware.

The logs ended up being quite useful for performance. For example, when trying to do optimizations for Intel GPUs, I noticed that some of the biggest shaders were being compiled in a non-optimal way. I basically ran the whole game in just 2 big shaders, one to blend the scene with all the quads, and another pass where I do lighting, shadows and effects like water, where the final normal and height map of the scene are presented. Because these shaders were so big, they couldn't be compiled for SIMD16.

These integrated Intel GPUs are quite common on laptops, and they can shade 16 pixels at once, but only if everything in the shader fits in a small amount of very fast memory. Because my shaders grew so much and I wasn't even aware that this would be an actual issue, the driver was quietly falling back to shading 8 pixels at a time, making the game run noticeably slower. Once I had this information in the logs, I could see what I needed to trim down. I reduced the number of values I needed to keep around as much as possible, while also avoiding duplicated code caused by things like macros until everything fit again.

During development I was always careful about how demanding the game was, but after switching to a faster computer I started paying less attention to it. It's quite easy to just settle for something that looks good enough and move on to the next thing when you're busy. That's why I started targeting the Steam Deck and aiming for stable 90 FPS. It helped me keep performance in sight and avoid things that would make the game too slow on low-powered platforms.

I feel like I threw away a lot of work during development because the art and design of the game changed several times. In hindsight, I think it was good to keep the mentality of avoiding things that would make the game slow and keeping an eye on the performance stats. But it was only towards the end of the game that I could simply focus on performance without worrying about optimizing things in a way that would make them hard to generalize or reuse in the future, since the game was finished.

In the end I actually added a performance mode that tones down a few special effects, but I think it was a good decision to do that when the game was finished. Otherwise, you suddenly need to be testing and tweaking more than one version of the game while making changes and adding new things.

A frame limiter was something else I added to help slower laptops maintain a stable framerate. This also brought the necessity of adding an option to draw the cursor in hardware. For the whole development I was drawing the cursor within the game in software, and that meant some lag was unavoidable. Many users complained about this when the demo was released.

This happens when you use Vsync because the last frame you're seeing is actually buffered, so the frame is already behind the input. The OS has a special mode for drawing the cursor that prevents these issues, but then you lose the ability to apply effects to it, like fluid animations or doing some lighting around it. Being aware of this also helped me focus on reducing the input lag of the game as much as possible. When running the game with the frame limiter, you notice immediately that the cursor becomes super laggy. For that case, having a hardware cursor was necessary.

Looking back on all these details, being able to change basic engine things like that is super hard, or almost impossible, with closed engines. I worked with Unity before, doing some ports, and the mentality there was that you had to follow a set of "good practices" and deal with whatever was decided for you, even though the hardware in most cases could do better. It was very rough and slow at the beginning when making a custom engine, but the freedom you get at the end of development is very satisfying.

I feel lucky I got the chance to take this long road and actually make it to the end. I stumbled into something really interesting, and had so many moments of realization while working on this project that I lost count.

After all these years, I'm quite happy now to have found the perfect excuse to actually study the things I love the most to work on.

If you enjoyed this article, consider giving Satelital a try. The game is available on Steam, with a free demo available.

#9980. UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Britain's new Labour-led government is making a concerted push to get ahead of the AI risks to its national networks and the industrial complex.

At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure.

His Majesty's Government broadcast its cybersecurity agenda on Nov. 3, releasing a variety of policy papers, an annual report from its lead cybersecurity agency, and related announcements pertaining to the security of small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs), supply chain vendors, critical national infrastructure (CNI), and more. These items all followed from an updated Autumn Budget 2026, released last week, which provisioned nearly two hundred billion pounds for AI-driven government cybersecurity projects.

Amid all of the practical policy updates, the headline quote of the day came from the state's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which assessed that it's "highly likely that between now and 2028, AI‑powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI." It also labeled "highly likely" the prospect that "China, Russia, and other nation states will routinely use AI cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals" in the country.

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

In a new report, Manchester-based NCC Group polled Members of Parliament (MPs) about the state of the UK's CNI cybersecurity posture. About half (51%) of MPs reported that their areas of the country are "not keeping pace" with the threats to its infrastructure. Only 22% expressed confidence in their country's posture. Asked about the nation's ability to fight off a major attack against its CNI, 47% believe that it's unprepared, whereas 41% feel it is.

The survey data is best read as aspirational, not prescriptive. There's little evidence that the UK is less prepared than other nations in addressing threats to its critical infrastructure, or that politicians would be able to tell one way or the other. Leaders are simply aware of the magnitude of what faces them.

"The challenge isn't a lack of government action; it's proof that action translates into resilience," says Katharina Sommer, head of government affairs at NCC Group. "There's still no tested blueprint for coordinating cyber response effectively across government and industry, and that’s not a problem unique to the UK. The test for critical infrastructure operators is whether they can demonstrate, before an attack hits, that they can sustain essential services, recover quickly and maintain public confidence," which remains an open question.

A clearer message came through on Nov. 3, from the experts at the NCSC. Using a scale in which "likely" accords with roughly 55% to 75% odds, "highly likely" with 80% to 90% odds, and "almost certain" approaching 100%, it bet that it is:

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

Likely that threat actors will use AI cyber tools to needle vulnerabilities in CNI

Highly likely that nation-states will use AI to increase the speed and sophistication of their cyberattacks, in service of their geopolitical goals in the UK; in particular, the agency identified China as the foremost player in terms of intent and capability to hit CNI and other strategic targets

Almost certain that "many systems will remain vulnerable" to AI-empowered attacks

The NCSC also drew out some future scenarios. Optimistically, it acknowledged that AI-driven cyber threat development might slow, allowing a window of time for the UK to catch up with the problem. Pessimistically, it painted a picture in which AI threats totally outpace the UK's ability to keep up.

"The situation is likely to be worse than is currently known, with many variables and unknowns still to be discovered," according to the report.

The message out of the UK government on Tuesday was, more or less: we're trying to get ahead of this.

In a policy paper, the government acknowledged that 2018's Network and Information Systems (NIS) Regulations — the UK's only multisector cybersecurity law — is "out of date and insufficient to tackle the threats we face." In a speech announcing its Annual Review 2026, NCSC CEO Richard Horne called the law built to replace NIS 2018 — November 2025's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — "a vital step forward." The updated bill brings data centers, managed service providers (MSPs), and specific "critical suppliers" into the fold, and introduces stricter breach reporting requirements and hefty fines for negligence.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

In a separate policy paper concerning the same bill, the government stated its intention to introduce a new vendor risk management framework focused specifically on the "national security risks posed by vendors" connected to essential service providers. And in yet a third, related paper, the government described how the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will be used to account for agentic "loss of control" incidents, in the fashion of this summer's AI industry lab leaks. Projected future measures include:

Security and resilience requirements to prevent loss of control incidents

Empowering ministers to perform postmortems

The bill is currently passing through Parliament.

Besides this one bill, the UK government also announced £2.4 billion in subsidies to help micro-, small, and medium-sized businesses attain "Cyber Essentials" certifications. All of this week's announcements come on the heels of an Autumn Budget last week, which arranged for tens of billions of pounds each to fund, among other things:

A National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, for vulnerability discovery across the country, including CNI

A National Cyber Shield, for training AI agents to automate cyber defense

A separate National Agentic Security Unit for fighting rogue AI agents

"Increasing the funding and focus on cybersecurity to help keep the UK secure is very welcome," says Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence for KnowBe4. At the same time, he adds, "the main challenge I see is scale."

"£154 million for cyber-defenses is a good step," he believes, "but the NCSC estimates cyberattacks cost UK organizations £14.7 billion a year."

Dark Reading asked cybersecurity experts what governments like the UK's need to do to prevent future worst-case scenarios. They consistently emphasized the same point:

"AI did not create new weaknesses; it revealed them. Most incidents still start through the same familiar routes, such as phishing, stolen credentials, and the traditional kill chain paths attackers have relied on for years. The key to stopping these threats is, surprisingly, not exciting: it's the fundamentals," Chapman argues.

The fundamentals for Graham Taylor CBE, director of defense strategy for Northern Europe at OPSWAT, start with protecting the edge. "Too many critical sites rely on firewalls and VPNs for connections that only need to send data one way. Where a facility only exports monitoring data, a hardware-enforced data diode removes the return path entirely, so neither a human attacker nor AI can use that link to send commands into the facility," he says.

Jacob Krell, Suzu Labs senior director for secure AI solutions and cybersecurity, emphasizes network segmentation "built like a boat." AI is going to make the perimeter easier to breach, he says, "and it cuts the time to objective once an attacker is inside. Critical infrastructure is notoriously vulnerable here because operators are hesitant to patch and test systems, and their caution is rational; a bad update takes a plant offline. So the perimeter fails more often and the interior offers nothing to slow lateral movement."

John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, tosses out a less conventional suggestion for fighting off AI threats to CNI. "If AI gives attackers the ability to do a tremendous amount of work very quickly, defenders have an opportunity to present them with large numbers of decoys to investigate," he says. "We need creative ways to make those decoys look realistic and dynamic. The more time attacking AI agents spend interacting with decoys, the less time they spend attacking real systems."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9979. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎

Open weights for image editing, generation and layouts

#9977. Windows 11 collects data on which coding agents and dev tools you use

I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe, and cursor.exe, alongside familiar developer tools such as python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, and code.exe.

Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools?

The names were in MissionControlAggregator.dll. I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. And unless you have opted out of the “optional” diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), the data is uploaded to Microsoft.

I shared the initial finding on X. This post includes more details about the investigation behind it.

Opening the DLL in Binary Ninja made the first lead easy to see. These were explicit executable names embedded in a Windows component:

Following the references showed that the names were used in comparisons. There are four CLI-agent slots checking copilot.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, and agy.exe, with extensionless equivalents on the WSL route. Five desktop-agent slots check github.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, cursor.exe, and antigravity.exe.

Here is one of the comparisons against codex.exe:

The compiler-generated C++ names are unwieldy, so I will call these functions executable-name matchers. For reference, one related matcher is std::_Func_impl_no_alloc<, bool, std::basic_string_view> const&, Microsoft::Diagnostics::MissionControlAggregator::Utils::AppType>::_Do_call. The screenshot shows another lambda instantiation performing the same kind of name comparison.

The feature guarding the new agent checks has a particularly direct name: CLICodingAgentUsage, feature ID 62580080.

And the list extends beyond AI agents. The same component checks for node.exe, python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, clang.exe, gdb.exe, javac.exe, devenv.exe, and code.exe, among others. Those checks feed broader developer-tool categories. Some of these checks also verify the publisher: the Node.js slot expects Node.js Foundation, Python expects Python Software Foundation, and the .NET and Visual Studio slots expect Microsoft Corporation. The compiler/debugger group containing GCC and Clang has no additional publisher check in this path.

For Windows programs, it consumes KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary and Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary. These provide application identities that its handlers parse and pass to the matchers. For WSL, it consumes Microsoft.Windows.Lxss.Manager.Exec and ExecCritical, using the imageName field. A regular Windows codex.exe can therefore reach the CLI-agent checks through the app-state summary route; this is not limited to Linux programs running inside WSL.

A successful match sets a slot in the aggregator’s state. Later, ReportCohorts<12,4,5> turns those slots into bitsets and emits a report named Segments.SubCohorts. The numbers correspond to twelve broader tool categories, four CLI agents, and five desktop agents.

ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) is the mechanism carrying that report. In this case, it is a self-describing TraceLogging event. Rather than writing the executable names into every report, the component assigns each category a bit. A set Codex bit means the matching tool was observed during the reporting window.

The source events also include runtime, time in focus, interaction counters, and resource usage. This component appears to discard those details and record only a bitmap of which agents were observed. The report’s timestamps describe the collection window, not how long each agent was used.

Strings and code are a useful lead, but I wanted to see the component running. I checked my Parallels Windows 11 ARM64 VM, build 26200.9974. Its MissionControlAggregator.dll was version 10.0.26100.9818, and CLICodingAgentUsage was already enabled as a service experiment. I had not manually enabled the feature.

DiagTrack, the Connected User Experiences and Telemetry service, was also already running with its startup type set to Automatic. It starts a separate AggregatorHost.exe process, and that process loads the DLL. The following administrative PowerShell commands show the service, its child process, and the loaded module:

The process IDs connect the pieces: DiagTrack runs in process 10148, which is the parent of AggregatorHost.exe, process 1500; the module listing places MissionControlAggregator.dll inside that child.

To test the finding in practice, I copied cmd.exe to a file named codex.exe and ran it in the interactive Windows session. The name alone was enough for the component to recognize it as Codex.

I captured an AppStateChangeSummary for the running process from the KernelProcess provider ({2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}), with LaunchCount=1 and TerminateCount=0. The aggregator’s saved state contained the value 2 in CLI slot 2, the Codex slot. A separate run without an additional ETW trace also set that slot, confirming that detection worked through Windows’ existing diagnostic collection.

The report normally follows a roughly daily boundary. To capture it immediately, I temporarily moved the saved reporting-window start 25 hours into the past and restarted DiagTrack with a trace listening for the aggregator. The resulting Segments.SubCohorts event contained:

The value 4 is 1 << 2: the Codex CLI bit. The name had made it through the input summary, the matcher, the persisted state, and the emitted report.

I also tested the developer-tool path separately, using a copy of cmd.exe named gcc.exe. It set developer-tool slot 3. With optional diagnostic data allowed, I found the resulting Segments.SubCohorts event in DiagTrack’s upload queue with SubCohorts: [8] (1 << 3). This is the compiler/debugger category shared by GCC, Clang, and related tools, rather than a separate bit for each executable.

An ETW event by itself would not establish that anything leaves the machine. ETW is used for plenty of local diagnostics. The more revealing question was who was listening to this particular report.

The first subscription, for KernelProcess, had MatchAnyKeyword=0x400000000002, which includes the summary’s 0x400000000000 keyword. The second, for Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator, had MatchAnyKeyword=0xe00000000000, which includes the report’s 0x800000000000 keyword. Both had level 255.

The subscription showed where the report could go. To check whether Windows actually queued it for transmission, I inspected DiagTrack’s EventStore.db and decompressed the JSON batches in its AsimovEvents table. This revealed an important condition: the agent-usage report is treated as optional diagnostic data.

When optional diagnostic data is allowed (enabled by default in the US setup I tested), Windows queues the coding-agent usage report for upload to Microsoft. I verified this by finding the agent event itself in DiagTrack’s upload queue:
