#9855. Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Two AI agents, separately over a five-day period, autonomously tried to access connected applications, including Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, and GitHub, without account owner permission.

Grok Bots attempted to access corporate applications without their users' approval or knowledge, presenting yet another security challenge for enterprises as AI agents become increasingly autonomous.

Researchers at NewCore identified 31 unprompted attempts by two xAI Grok Bots to access connected corporate applications over a five-day period, including Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, GitHub, and Notion, according to the findings of an investigation published today. In one case, the bot continued making background requests even after its owner had declined offers for recurring check-ins four times.

The requests were not approved and did not reach the underlying corporate data: NewCore had placed a security gateway between the agents and the applications, requiring human approval for each request.

"Over five days, two Grok Bots on NewCore employee accounts made 31 requests to calendar, email, Slack, GitHub and Notion while nobody was talking to them, some with the laptop shut," Ido Hoorvitch, security research team lead at NewCore, wrote in the report.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

One bot repeatedly attempted to retrieve Google Calendar events in the evening, overnight, and the following day, despite there being no active conversation with its owner. In a second case, another bot attempted to access Notion's calendar tools before Google Calendar had even been connected. It continued making requests while its owner's laptop was closed and asleep.

The investigation began as an internal experiment at NewCore, which wanted to understand how autonomous AI agents behave when connected to real corporate systems. The company earlier this year provided employees with enterprise Grok Bot accounts and connected the agents to corporate services, including email, calendars, Notion, and other business applications.

However, NewCore put a handbrake in place: It did not give the agents unrestricted, standing access to company data. Instead, requests had to pass through its Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway. The gateway sent an approval notification to the employee who owned the account whenever a Grok Bot tried to access an application. If a request was not approved within three minutes, it automatically expired and was denied, Hoorvitch said.

"We did it because we had no way to audit why an agent reaches for data, and until we do, the gate stays closed by default," he wrote. Ultimately, this security control allowed NewCore to observe and reconstruct the bots' background activity.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

The first sign that something was amiss came after an employee used Grok Bot to retrieve their daily calendar, approving the request through the gateway as expected. Later that evening, however, the gateway recorded further calendar access attempts, despite the employee no longer interacting with the bot.

This led investigators to uncover repeated attempts by Grok agents to access corporate applications without any corresponding user interaction. Moreover, when one bot was asked whether it had made the gateway calls, it said it had not, Hoorvitch said. The requests did not appear in the bot's chat history.

"It was telling the truth. … That is the part to sit with," he wrote. "An agent that cannot account for its own actions is not a bug report. It is a finding."

NewCore contacted xAI about its findings and said the company's support team confirmed that the activity was not the result of a software vulnerability or an exploit, but was part of Grok Bot's built-in background check-in functionality.

"These are built-in background check-ins by the primary bot, during a check-in the bot looks at its connected sources, and there is no user or admin setting to turn them off," Hoorvitch wrote, relaying the response from xAI support.

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

According to NewCore, xAI also said that customers seeking to stop the check-ins could send the vendor a list of employee sign-in addresses. NewCore said it had not received an official response from xAI's media team at the time the report was published.

The lack of a user- or administrator-facing setting to disable background check-ins, or to control which connected tools they can use, creates a visibility and governance challenge for security teams. Employees may not know when an AI agent is accessing connected applications, while the agent itself may not retain a record of its server-initiated activity in the chat history visible to its owner.

"The danger is not that the model goes rogue," Hoorvitch explains to Dark Reading. "The concern is that we hand agents standing credentials and then let someone else decide when they act. The owner thinks the bot works when they talk to it. The vendor thinks a helpful bot checks in on its own. The model does what the platform tells it in that turn, not what the owner would have said."

Though "nobody in that chain is malicious," he says, "the result is still a bot reading your inbox at 7:46 a.m. while you are asleep."

The distinction matters because all 31 unattended requests identified by NewCore were read operations, such as retrieving calendar events or searching messages, Hoorvitch explains. None resulted in data being accessed, because the gateway blocked them. However, the same connected tool sets included capabilities to take actions, such as sending email, modifying calendar events, and posting Slack messages. NewCore warned that the same background processes could pose a greater risk if they were to invoke those write-capable tools.

In NewCore's investigation, its MCP gateway blocked all 31 unattended requests. The company argues that organizations need similar independent controls to set and enforce policies on AI agents operating within their systems.

"Put the decision outside the agent," Hoorvitch says. "Route every agent tool call through something you own, like the NewCore MCP Gateway, where the owner's policy decides what goes through and every call is logged whether or not the agent remembers it."

NewCore also recommends that organizations immediately inventory the agents connected to corporate tools, identify which applications and data they can reach, and assign an owner to each. Security teams should review not only approved activity but also requests that were denied or left unanswered, since these can reveal what agents attempt to do without user involvement.

"Most teams cannot answer that today," Hoorvitch says, "and you cannot govern what you cannot list."

They cover planning, debugging, code review, architecture, refactors and deploys, and they're packaged as the Dev Workflow plugin in Cuttlefish.MD, HackerNoon's license-checked skills marketplace.

An agent skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file of instructions, plus any scripts or references it needs. The agent loads it only when a task calls for it. The format is an open standard at agentskills.io that 32+ tools support, including Claude Code and Codex CLI.

#9853. Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

A compromised key issued to AI infrastructure provider Fireworks was used by threat actors to access Cursor data and credentials.

Cursor has traced the origins of a security incident involving a malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in its marketplace to a breach at AI infrastructure provider Fireworks.

As many as 5,000 users may have downloaded the tampered extension during the roughly 11 hours it was live on Oct. 29. It was a reminder of the risk organizations face when they rely on third-party marketplaces for software applications and extensions. It also illustrates how one security lapse can lead to a cascade of subsequent breaches and supply chain attacks.

When Cursor first disclosed the incident, the company said attackers had placed malicious versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in a cache serving its Visual Studio (VS) Code extension marketplace. Users who requested either of two specific cached versions of the extension (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) during the exposure window may have downloaded the malicious builds, the company said. The malicious extensions attempted to collect information about infected systems and establish persistent remote access, including by installing an attacker-controlled SSH key.

Related:Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Cursor quickly removed the malicious extensions, temporarily shut down its marketplace, and audited the store for signs of further tampering. Cursor also rotated its keys, rebuilt the marketplace, and worked with the cloud provider hosting the attacker's server to take it offline. The company's initial advisory, however, did not explain how the attacker might have gained access to its environment and planted the malicious extension in its extensions marketplace.

In an update on Nov. 13, Cursor filled in that blank, with a detailed description of what its investigation had unearthed in the days following the Oct. 29 incident.

Some of the stored session records contained credentials that had not been properly redacted. The attacker used those credentials to access what Cursor described as select SaaS tools for accessing non-production source code repositories, customer support data, emails, usage metrics, and other data.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

On Oct. 29, the attacker subsequently used one of the compromised credentials to tamper with the cache that Cursor uses to deliver extensions through its VS Code marketplace. The attacker inserted unauthorized copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in the marketplace where they remained available to users for about 11 hours.

"Anthropic did not publish this copy, and this was not a vulnerability in Anthropic's product," Cursor stressed in its update. "The marketplace source, Open VSX, never had the malware. At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions of the extension on October 29 potentially received the malicious build."

Cursor estimated that API credentials belonging to fewer than 0.01% of its customers were exposed in the incident. Historical coding-agent session records, or traces, belonging to fewer than 0.05% of users were accessed, the company said.

However, the supply chain attack goes back even further than Fireworks, which itself was a victim of a third-party breach. In a Nov. 9 update, Fireworks said a cloud provider hosting the AI company's R&D systems "experienced a security incident on Oct. 23." The attackers used the access to the R&D systems to obtain sensitive data, including API keys and access tokens.

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

According to Fireworks, the available evidence linked the breach of its environment to a financially motivated cybercriminal group seeking to monetize unauthorized access to large language models. It's a practice known as LLMjacking, which Google and others have described as a rapidly emerging threat for organizations across multiple sectors in North America, Asia-Pacific, and other regions.

Following the incident, Cursor said it has implemented a broad security overhaul to reduce the risk of similar compromises. Immediate steps the company has taken include cutting off Firework's access to all its shared data sets, revoking and replacing potentially exposed credentials, and rotating internal credentials. The company has also tightened restrictions on how its systems and third-party service providers can communicate with one another and expanded automated scanning for secrets across its code repositories and internal data.

The Cursor incident is another indication of how the rapid adoption of AI-powered development tools and increasingly interconnected software ecosystems has exacerbated software supply chain risks. Recently, for instance, researchers uncovered more than 550 exposed secrets in Microsoft VS Code and Open VSX extension packages, including over 100 publishing tokens that could have allowed attackers to distribute malicious updates to legitimate extensions. Similarly, earlier this year researchers identified dozens of malicious GlassWorm VS Code extensions seeded in the Open VSX marketplace to steal developer credentials that attackers could use to spread poisoned software packages.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9852. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997

Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

"Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.

Nobody thinks that, literally. What I mean by that is, nothing capable of thinking would have written this sentence down because no thinking entity would suspect that decision models originated probabilistic classification. Only a non-thinking source of language, such as an LLM, might generate this sentence.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Again, nobody thinks that, meaning only an LLM might generate this sentence.

The state + questions interface carries over to hosted decision models too. meraGPT Decider 1.1 takes the same shape through an API (model decider-1.1) rather than as open weights: up to 255 options per choice question, images in the state, and if you offer an "I don't know" option it takes it when the state doesn't support an answer. Against TypeSafe Jev 1.14 on the same items it's ahead on typed decisions, calibration and large label sets. Input is $0.04 per million tokens and output is free.

Release notes: https://meragpt.com/blog/introducing-decider-1-1?utm_source=huggingface&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=hf_decision_blog

#9851. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9850. How Cash Withdrawal Limits, CTRs, and Anti-Money Laundering Rules Work

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Walk up to a commercial bank counter on a Tuesday morning and ask to withdraw USD 10,000 of your own money to buy a used pickup truck or pay a roofing contractor. Your paycheck has been landing in that checking account every two weeks for a decade. You have a valid driver’s license in your hand, zero debt on the account, and a cleared balance twice the size of your request. Instead of counting out hundreds, a 22-year-old teller freezes, stares at the monitor, and starts interrogating you like a narcotics detective: What are you buying? Who is the seller? Why do they want cash? Do you have a signed invoice?

After 25 years working inside commercial banks, I can tell you that customer rage at the teller window almost always comes from a single misunderstanding. Everyday depositors genuinely believe a checking account is a digital safety deposit box holding their physical money. When you ask for a thick stack of hundred-dollar or hundred-euro bills, three invisible banking realities collide behind that counter at the exact same moment: the legal nature of your account balance, the brutal unit economics of branch vault cash, and a federal compliance machine that punishes banks with billion-dollar fines if they fail to pry into your personal business.

The hardest truth for retail banking customers to swallow is that the money sitting in your checking account does not belong to you anymore. The instant you hand physical banknotes across a counter or receive a direct-deposit paycheck, legal title to those funds passes entirely to the banking corporation.

Under foundational banking law going all the way back to the landmark 1848 English House of Lords decision in Foley v. Hill, a standard bank deposit creates a debtor-creditor relationship rather than a legal bailment. If you hand your winter coat to a restaurant coat-check attendant, that attendant is a bailee who must guard your specific coat and return that exact garment when you hand over your ticket. A commercial bank operates under the exact opposite legal structure. It takes absolute ownership of the currency you deposit, mixes those funds into its general balance sheet, and issues you an unsecured IOU in return.

The Bank of England’s foundational research on modern money creation lays out how far removed everyday banking is from the public’s piggy-bank fantasy. Commercial banks create the vast majority of broad money out of thin air whenever they issue new loans, crediting a borrower’s account with brand-new digital deposit liabilities rather than moving piles of paper currency from a saver’s locker to a borrower’s hands. Your digital account balance is simply an accounting entry recording how much the bank owes you as an unsecured creditor, backed up to statutory limits by government deposit insurance.

When you stand at the window demanding USD 10,000 in physical bills, you are calling in a debt. Worse yet, from the bank’s operational perspective, you are forcing the institution to extinguish a cheap, weightless digital liability on its own ledger and hand over scarce physical central-bank notes from its asset column.

Hollywood heist movies have convinced the public that every suburban bank branch sits on top of a steel vault packed floor-to-ceiling with shrink-wrapped bricks of hundred-dollar bills. Back when I reviewed regional branch balance sheets, the reality looked a lot less cinematic. To a modern bank treasurer, physical paper currency sitting inside a branch vault is a dead asset that bleeds money every single hour it sits on the shelf.

Start with the opportunity cost of idle paper. A stack of twenty-dollar bills locked inside a neighborhood branch safe earns a flat zero percent yield. Digital reserves held electronically at the central bank, by contrast, generate risk-free daily income under the Federal Reserve’s interest on reserve balances framework and parallel European Central Bank deposit facilities. Every dollar or euro of paper cash sitting in a suburban branch is a dollar or euro that cannot sit at the central bank earning overnight interest.

On top of lost yield, physical currency carries heavy carrying costs. Vault cash must be insured against armed robbery and internal theft, counted under dual-custody camera protocols, reconciled every evening, and trucked across town by private cash-in-transit vendors like Brink’s or Loomis. Armored transport companies charge steep fees for every scheduled stop and even steeper surcharges for emergency off-cycle cash drops.

To protect profit margins, commercial banks run aggressive cash-minimization algorithms across their branch networks. Software tracks historical foot traffic, local retail store change orders, ATM cassette depletion rates, and seasonal payday spikes to calculate the bare minimum vault inventory a branch needs to survive until the next armored truck arrives. Many suburban branches carry surprisingly thin working buffers of large-denomination notes once you subtract the cash locked inside their automated teller machines and time-delay teller dispensers. Walk in unannounced on a Friday afternoon asking for USD 15,000 in crisp hundreds, and the branch manager panics because handing you that stack might literally wipe out the branch’s weekend operating float. Rather than admitting that a multi-billion-dollar financial institution only keeps a shoestring supply of paper bills on the premises, embarrassed staff often hide behind vague policy excuses or aggressive questioning.

Even when the vault has plenty of hundred-dollar bills sitting on the shelf, your withdrawal still has to clear the compliance panopticon running on the teller’s terminal. In the United States, any physical cash transaction (whether a deposit, a withdrawal, or a currency exchange) totaling more than USD 10,000 in a single business day triggers a mandatory filing with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) under the Bank Secrecy Act.

Under the federal banking agencies’ Currency Transaction Reporting examination manual, this USD 10,000.01 trigger is hardwired into core banking software and aggregates all cash activity conducted by or on behalf of the same person across every branch and ATM in the bank’s domestic network on the same business day. Pulling USD 6,000 from a teller window at 10:00 a.m. and another USD 4,500 from a branch three miles away at 2:00 p.m. automatically merges into a single USD 10,500 cash event that requires a Currency Transaction Report (CTR).

Here is what nobody tells you at the counter: a CTR is completely harmless. Millions of CTRs are filed electronically every year, and the form itself does not require you to bring in a bill of sale for a boat or prove why you want physical currency. All the teller legally needs to complete a CTR is your verified government ID, your Social Security or taxpayer identification number, and basic profile details such as your occupation.

Why, then, does the teller interrogate you about your kitchen remodel when you ask for USD 6,000 or USD 10,000? Because the CTR is only half of the surveillance architecture. The real minefield behind the counter is the Suspicious Activity Report (SAR).

Under the federal Suspicious Activity Reporting compliance rules, banks are legally required to flag any transaction of USD 5,000 or more that appears to have no apparent lawful purpose, deviates from a customer’s normal historical behavior, or looks designed to evade reporting rules. Frontline bank tellers do not ask nosy questions because they care about your used car. They ask because their screen pops up a mandatory compliance prompt whenever an out-of-pattern cash withdrawal is keyed in, and they cannot clear the screen without typing an explanation into the audit log.

Banks enforce these scripts with paranoid intensity because federal regulators destroy institutions that let suspicious cash slip through unchallenged. Look no further than October 2024, when FinCEN assessed a record USD 1.3 billion penalty against TD Bank as part of a massive USD 3 billion criminal and civil enforcement crackdown after the bank failed to monitor suspicious branch cash activity and file accurate reports. When executives watch a top-ten bank get hit with billion-dollar fines and regulatory asset caps, they pass ferocious pressure down to branch managers and USD 18-an-hour tellers.

If you get angry at the window, snap that "it is none of your damn business what I do with my own money," or change your story mid-sentence, the teller will usually smile politely and hand you your cash anyway. Then, the moment you walk out the glass doors, that teller clicks an internal referral box on their workstation to alert the bank’s financial intelligence unit.

And you will never know it happened. Under federal anti-tipping-off laws codified at 31 U.S.C. 5318(g)(2), any bank director, officer, or employee is strictly prohibited by law from notifying a customer that a Suspicious Activity Report has been prepared or filed. If a teller whispers to you that refusing to answer their question will trigger a government report, that teller commits a federal offense.

Customers across the European Union and the United Kingdom run into the exact same wall of suspicion, even though Europe does not use the American mechanical USD 10,000 CTR form in the same way. Under the European Union’s Anti-Money Laundering Directive framework, commercial banks must apply continuous risk-based customer due diligence across all accounts, monitor for unusual cash velocity, and obey strict statutory prohibitions against tipping off customers when filing suspicious transaction reports with national financial intelligence units.

In Europe, withdrawing cash from your branch is only half the legal battle; spending it can also trip statutory wires. Under the landmark 2024 EU Anti-Money Laundering Regulation, the bloc introduced an EU-wide maximum cap of EUR 10,000 on cash payments for goods or services in commercial transactions (applying across member states from July 2027), while explicitly allowing individual member states like France, Spain, and Italy to maintain much tighter national limits that already sit between EUR 1,000 and EUR 5,000. Even when a private peer-to-peer sale remains lawful, European branch compliance software flags sudden EUR 8,000 or EUR 12,000 cash withdrawals automatically, demanding source-of-funds and purpose-of-withdrawal notes before the teller releases the banknotes.

Once ordinary people learn about the USD 10,000 reporting threshold or experience an annoying interrogation at the counter, human nature kicks in. They decide to outsmart the bureaucracy.

Say a homeowner needs USD 14,000 in cash to buy a classic car from a private seller over the weekend. Wanting to avoid government forms and nosy teller questions, they decide to pull out USD 4,800 on Wednesday, USD 4,800 on Thursday, and USD 4,400 on Friday. Or maybe they pull USD 9,000 at the counter and walk outside to pull the remaining USD 1,500 from the ATM over the next two days.

Speaking as someone who spent two and a half decades inside the banking system, let me be blunt: this is the single dumbest financial mistake a law-abiding citizen can make.

Breaking up a large cash withdrawal or deposit into smaller chunks to stay underneath the USD 10,000 reporting radar is a standalone federal felony known as "structuring" (or smurfing in street slang). Under 31 U.S.C. 5324 of the United States Code, it is a federal crime punishable by up to five years in federal prison and steep fines to structure, assist in structuring, or attempt to structure any transaction with one or more domestic financial institutions for the purpose of evading currency reporting requirements.

Notice what is missing from that statute: the government does not have to prove that your money came from drug trafficking, tax fraud, or illegal gambling. As detailed in the U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Resource Manual on structuring, Congress amended the law in 1994 so prosecutors only need to show that you knew about the bank’s reporting obligation and intentionally split your transactions to prevent the bank from filing a CTR. Even if every single penny in your checking account came from your taxed W-2 salary as a high school teacher, splitting a USD 12,000 cash withdrawal into two USD 6,000 trips to dodge the paperwork turns an innocent withdrawal into a federal crime.

Worse still, bank transaction-monitoring algorithms are specifically engineered to catch this exact pattern. Every night, automated velocity filters scan across accounts looking for clustered cash withdrawals or deposits sitting between USD 3,000 and USD 9,900 over rolling seven-day, fourteen-day, and thirty-day windows. Taking out USD 14,000 in a single lump sum generates a boring, routine CTR that nobody at the bank looks at twice. Taking out USD 4,800 three days in a row trips the bank’s anti-structuring alarm, generates a mandatory SAR to FinCEN, and very often leads the bank’s risk committee to abruptly close your accounts and mail you a cashier’s check for your remaining balance, a practice insiders call "de-risking" or debanking.

In recent years, banks in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Europe have added a powerful new justification for grilling customers at the counter: protecting you from yourself.

To be completely fair to my former industry, social-engineering fraud against bank customers has exploded to staggering levels. Criminals running courier scams, romance frauds, and fake government-agent stings routinely coach elderly victims to walk into their local branch, demand USD 20,000 in physical cash, and lie to the teller by claiming the money is for roof repairs or a nephew’s wedding. In April 2024, FinCEN’s financial trend analysis on elder financial exploitation revealed that financial institutions filed 155,415 reports flagging roughly USD 27 billion in suspicious activity linked to elder scams and theft in just a single twelve-month window.

At the same time, regulators have begun shifting the financial cost of fraud directly onto bank balance sheets. In the United Kingdom, the Payment Systems Regulator launched its mandatory APP scam reimbursement framework in October 2024, forcing sending and receiving payment firms to split the cost of reimbursing victims tricked into sending fraudulent Faster Payments and CHAPS transfers. Across the UK, branch staff also operate under the Banking Protocol, an emergency escalation system where tellers silently summon local police to the branch if they believe a customer is withdrawing funds under the spell of a scammer.

When regulators punish banks financially and reputationally for failing to stop scams, banks react the only way large bureaucracies know how: they treat every customer over the age of fifty asking for cash like a confused ward of the state. I have watched sharp, retired business owners get stonewalled for forty-five minutes by a branch supervisor demanding to see text messages, contractor licenses, or vehicle registration papers before releasing USD 8,000 of the customer’s own savings. What started as a sensible shield against criminal coercion has mutated into paternalistic gatekeeping where grown adults have to beg a corporate bureaucracy for permission to spend their own money.

You cannot rewrite federal anti-money-laundering statutes at the teller window, and picking a philosophical fight with a frontline clerk will only get your account flagged for compliance review. What you can do is work the banking plumbing like an insider so you walk out with your cash cleanly, quickly, and without a SAR attached to your name:

Your bank owes you a debt, and you have every legal right to collect it in physical currency. Understand the mechanics behind the bulletproof glass, let the institution file its routine government forms, and never let the fear of routine paperwork trick you into structuring your own money.

#9849. 'TheMailer' Phishing Kit Puts AI in the Driver's Seat

The commercial kit uses attacker-supplied AI models to personalize lures, evade spam filters, and scale campaigns to tens of thousands of targets.

A new phishing kit is capable of orchestrating most elements of the attack through AI functionality, including tailoring email lures specifically to bypass content filters.

That's according to new Varonis research detailing "TheMailer," a phishing kit that leverages large language models (LLM) to a degree hardly seen in the cybercriminal ecosystem. Phishing kits and phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platforms have gained significant popularity in recent years, and AI has only made them more capable. To date, phishing kit AI functionality focuses mostly on generating lures, coding realistic phishing websites, conducting reconnaissance, and automating simple repetitive tasks.

TheMailer distinguishes itself in two primary ways. One, it automates much of the phishing process from end to end using the attacker's chosen AI model. Two, as Varonis senior security researcher Daniel Kelley wrote in the blog post, the kit can tailor lures to each mail provider and "rewrite them until they bypass spam filters."

Related:Anthropic Finds Ingredients for Future AI Worms

The attacker's "customer journey" begins by buying a lifetime license for between $3,000 and $6,000 in cryptocurrency (depending on the deal and which AI functions are included). The customer operator then plugs in their API key, selects an AI model (Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Grok, Gemini, and Mistral are included), and then they're more or less ready to start conducting campaigns. Kelley noted that customers only need to bring SMTP servers, proxies, and target email lists.

TheMailer can generate lures from a short prompt or a real brand email, personalize the emails for each recipient (including email address, body, and subject line), remove AI writing patterns, and adjust content for spam filters.

Kelley tells Dark Reading the kit is built to scale against targets.

"The seller's screenshots show a single campaign of nearly 25,000 emails and a list of more than 145,000 targets being sorted by mail provider. What's different is that every recipient gets their own version of the email, subject line, and attachment, so a bulk campaign no longer looks like one," he says. "I wouldn't call it a spear-phishing tool. The personalization we saw is at the level of a name on an invoice, and we didn't see features for researching individual targets. It's opportunistic phishing with the polish of something targeted."

It's unclear how successful the kit is — attacker LLM tools are historically capable of undertaking tasks at scale, but the success rates of these tasks vary — though Varonis assesses TheMailer to have a large customer base. Moreover, the kit may be a sign of things to come.

Related:New CUSTODY Framework Constrains AI Agents Inside the Network

"I'd expect more kits to follow," Kelley says, "because once one seller offers this, buyers start asking for it elsewhere."

For defenders, Varonis offered a few main recommendations. Because TheMailer is built specifically to get past content filters, organizations should consider email authentication practices like SPF, DKIM, and DMARC enforcement; monitoring for lookalike and new domains; and checking links through full redirect chains at the time of the click.

And when conducting phishing training, Varonis recommends making it reflect how emails look in a post-AI world.

"Bad grammar isn't a reliable sign anymore, so teach users to be wary of urgency, unexpected requests, and login prompts, especially 'unusual activity' or account statement alerts," the blog post read. Finally, "Least-privilege access and data monitoring limit the damage if someone clicks anyway."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9848. Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

#9847. AI Adoption Maturity Matrix (AAMM): The 5 Levels Every Organization Goes Through

AI Product Management & Growth · Built Ocupe.ai in 3 months, 96% workflow-hour reduction · Ex-Disney & YC · 2x Founder · 700+ professionals

AI Product Management & Growth · Built Ocupe.ai in 3 months, 96% workflow-hour reduction · Ex-Disney & YC · 2x Founder · 700+ professionals

AI Product Management & Growth · Built Ocupe.ai in 3 months, 96% workflow-hour reduction · Ex-Disney & YC · 2x Founder · 700+ professionals

Someone sends a launch announcement, a few people share prompts in a channel, and the board update says "we're using AI."

The reports take as long as they did before, the approvals still queue in the same inbox, and nobody can say what changed.

AI maturity shows up in how work moves, not in the software catalog. A leadership team can name every model, API, and vendor it has approved, while the people using those tools still handle work exactly as before. The tools exist. The workflow around them never got redesigned.

That gap is the real maturity gap, and it is organizational, not technical.

I have operated across all five levels described below, from running early pilots to shipping a production AI platform that cut human workflow hours by 96% on one marketing workflow. The pattern holds across every engagement: most leaders don't know this sequence exists, but their organizations are going through it anyway. Without a map, they mistake tool adoption for operating outcomes and call themselves further along than their workflows are.

The diagnostic I use for this is the AI Adoption Maturity Matrix (AAMM), an ordered, evidence-based assessment I developed across those engagements. The AAMM looks for changes in workflow design, human governance, and measurable operating results. Tool access, isolated enthusiasm, and a successful demo are explicitly not evidence of a level.

This article defines the five AAMM levels, names the level almost everyone skips, and gives you a short assessment to find out where your organization really stands.

Three patterns show up repeatedly in the readiness conversations I run with leadership teams.

The tool-adoption illusion. A team licenses a model, connects it to one tool, and reports "we're using AI" in the next board update. Nobody asks whether the workflow changed. It didn't.

Pilot theater. A pilot ships to a friendly internal audience, gets a positive reaction in a demo, and gets reported upward as a win. The demo audience isn't the production audience. The metrics that matter (error rate under real volume, time to approval, cost per completed output) were never measured.

The level-skip. This is the most expensive pattern. A team moves straight from experimentation to scaling a tool across more use cases, without ever doing the unglamorous work of mapping the workflow, separating judgment from mechanical effort, and assigning gate ownership. The scaling just multiplies the mess.

Each pattern shares a root cause: the organization assessed its AI maturity by counting tools instead of examining how work actually moves.

How leaders mistake it for something higher

People are actively testing AI tools. Activity may be informal, with no established process, metric, or accountable owner

"We're exploring AI" gets reported as "we're adopting AI"

A team runs a pilot that has an owner and a defined scope

A high output count gets mistaken for business value, and no one has written the exit criteria

The workflow has been mapped and redesigned around what AI can and cannot do, rather than AI being added to the old process

Most companies never reach this level. They believe Level 2 metrics already proved it

Human checkpoints have pre-defined stop criteria, a named owner, and a record of when each gate fired

Treated as the finish line, when it is the operating baseline

The workflow runs in production, results are measured from operational data, gates stay active, and findings feed continuous improvement

Rarely claimed, because it requires admitting Levels 1–4 were preparation, not the destination

Two things about this table matter more than the labels.

The levels are not one company-wide number. A team can run a Level 4 workflow in one department while another department sits at Level 1, so the AAMM is applied per workflow with the scope held constant between assessments. The company view is the spread of those results, because an average would hide exactly the level-skip described above. And Level 3 is where most initiatives die. It is the hardest level to sell internally because it produces no visible output: a workflow map, a risk classification, and a set of gate owners are unglamorous deliverables that look like a delay to an executive expecting a demo.

A Level 2 pilot asks whether the model can produce an acceptable draft. Level 3 asks a different question entirely: which decisions in this workflow require human judgment, which are mechanical, and who owns the point where the two meet?

That second question is harder than it sounds, because answering it means naming the workflow. Not the department, not the tool, the workflow. On the platform I operate, there are more than 55 of them, each named and scoped separately: video and lip-sync generation, calendar planning, the creative pipeline, lead generation with its CRM sync, and multi-provider content generation. None of that structure existed when the work was a Level 2 pilot. It came out of the mapping exercise, and the mapping exercise is the thing teams skip when they jump from a promising demo to a rollout.

Level 4 is governance that actually functions: every human checkpoint has pre-defined stop criteria, a named owner, and a record of when it fired. That last part is what most teams miss. A gate nobody logs is a gate nobody can audit, and a gate nobody can audit is a preference, not a control.

Level 5 adds measurement and the loop that follows from it. The workflow is in production, results come from operational data rather than a quarterly narrative, the gates stay active, and what the data shows feeds the next revision. In practice that means the quality standard lives in the system instead of in a reviewer's memory: 140+ named rules, QA checks, policies, and static gates, plus 72 hard-enforced channel limits across 51 channel and spec surfaces. A rule a reviewer has to remember to apply will eventually not get applied. A rule the system enforces doesn't have that failure mode.

That number came from Level 5, not Level 2. The first version of the system, the Level 2 pilot, produced fluent drafts that quietly violated brand rules nobody had documented, and it overwhelmed the reviewers it was supposed to help. Reaching the 96% result required mapping and redesigning the workflow (Level 3), putting gates with real stop criteria and named owners around it (Level 4), and then running it long enough on measured operational data to improve it (Level 5).

The method matters more than the number. That figure counts only the share of the job that happens on the platform, which is about a third of the benchmark. The other two thirds stay outside the claim, unmeasured time is held at the benchmark rather than scored as instant, and an overrun shows up as a negative number. A maturity level you can defend is mostly a measurement method you can defend.

A number like 96% is not proof that a company has "done AI." It is proof that one workflow climbed all five levels. Most AI headlines report Level 2 activity with Level 5 language.

Run this against one specific workflow, not your company as a whole.

Then ask the fifth one out loud, in the room: what happens when the model gets something wrong? Someone should answer in ten seconds. Name who catches it and what the fallback is. A pause is the finding. If two or more of these land below where you expected, the organization is not where its last board update said it was.

Use the levels to diagnose each workflow, then summarize the company as a distribution: how many workflows sit at each level, and which levels are empty. A single blended score would hide that one workflow can sit at Level 4 while five others stay at Level 1. Record the highest level whose evidence is actually present, and where evidence is missing, write down the lower demonstrated level and the specific gap. To choose where to start, compare candidate workflows by volume, risk, value delivered and hours currently lost. The AAMM locates maturity; those operating measures set priority.

One clarification worth making, because it is the most common misreading: the AAMM measures operational maturity, not how autonomous the system is. Level 5 means measured, accountable operation with human controls still active. It doesn't mean unsupervised.

The expensive mistake is not failing to adopt AI. It is reporting Level 2 activity as Level 4 maturity, and building a roadmap on top of a number that was never real.

Most organizations do not need another tool evaluation.

They need someone to walk into the room and ask who owns the workflow now, what decision still requires a human, and what the system does when it gets something wrong. A Level 5 workflow can answer those questions before a draft reaches its reviewer: the checks have run, the exceptions are visible, and the human decision is clear. That is what maturity looks like in operation.

Stop Asking Which AI Model to Use. Start Asking Who Owns the Output
