#9836. Crypto Market Cycles: Reading the Phases Before You Buy

Why do investors become eager to buy assets that attracted little interest before? The change often has as much to do with confidence as with the asset itself. You see that in bonds and shares, and in the enthusiasm and anxiety surrounding crypto.

When learning how to buy crypto, earlier cycles can help you judge those shifts and possible entry opportunities, even though they won't tell you exactly where prices go next.

Economic conditions and investors' changing expectations influence how much buying or selling pressure a market faces. Crypto can move through sharp changes quickly, though its cycles have no fixed duration. When buyers become less willing to meet sellers' prices, downward pressure can build. Interest may eventually return, beginning another advance.

The familiar cycle model groups this behaviour into accumulation, markup, distribution and markdown. Their boundaries are often clearer afterwards than while you are deciding what to do.

A severe sell-off leaves plenty of investors discouraged. Some give up their holdings, trading becomes quieter and prices may settle into a range well below the earlier highs. This is the setting described as accumulation. You can see that the market has fallen; you cannot yet know whether it has finished falling.

Patient value investors, including some large holders or whales, consider the depressed price worth accepting the risk. They build a position in anticipation of renewed interest.

As successive peaks exceed previous highs and pullbacks stop above earlier lows, the advance becomes easier to follow. This is the bull market described by the markup stage. Technically minded investors track the pattern, while media attention draws more people towards crypto. A temporary fall now looks to many buyers like a chance to enter the rising market.

More newcomers bring more trading, and the rise can continue even as prices become hard to justify on the asset's merits. Buyers start depending on someone else paying a higher price, which is the greater-fool argument rather than a judgement of value. As the advance loses momentum, people who hesitated earlier can rush in together, treating it as their chance to join the rally. That late burst of buying can send prices sharply higher.

After an extended rise, prices may stop making progress. Buyers expecting further gains meet holders who see little upside left and want to realise profits.

Trading can stay busy while prices fluctuate inside a range. Optimists regard the pause as preparation for another climb; pessimists see the advance running out of strength. With neither view settled, the confidence of the rising market gives way to uncertainty.

Markdown is the point at which the excitement of the rally turns into anxiety. To find a buyer, sellers may have to accept progressively lower prices, taking the market back towards levels it passed on the way up. People still buy, but demand at the earlier prices has weakened. Investors concerned with cutting losses can keep selling despite encouraging news, so good headlines alone may not stop the decline.

Selling after the decline has begun can mean accepting less profit than you had expected, or a larger loss on an already losing position. Holding leaves your return exposed to any further fall, although a recovery is also possible.

An accumulation label often comes with a bullish longer-term forecast; a distribution label can signal that an analyst expects weakness. Some forecasts also lean on the Bitcoin halving. This scheduled cut halves miners' subsidy of newly issued bitcoin once per 210,000 blocks, approximately every four years. Earlier rallies have encouraged comparisons with that rhythm, but a reduction in new issuance cannot guarantee the demand needed to sustain another rise.

A market with spot exchange-traded funds and more institutional involvement may behave differently from the markets in earlier charts. Changes in economic conditions or regulation can also disrupt comparisons, so examine a forecast's assumptions before treating its timing as a guide.

When prices have fallen and attention is elsewhere, use the quiet to investigate the projects you might want to hold for longer. Research gives you a reason for choosing an asset beyond its discount from an earlier peak. If you decide to build a position, buying gradually distributes your entry over several prices. You give up the task of finding the single lowest point, without gaining a promise of cheaper purchases overall or protection from losses.

During an advance, planned profit-taking gives you a way to realise gains without joining the rush to buy at ever higher prices. Keep risk controls in place and use the levels in your plan rather than chasing the latest peak. If momentum slows and peaks become lower, review the gains still exposed in your holdings and consider a more defensive position. A falling market calls for a different question: does your investment case still hold? Avoid a panic sale, but reduce exposure when your assessment warrants it, using the quieter period to learn and rebalance.

You can investigate while interest is low, recognise the enthusiasm behind a rise and review your exposure as confidence starts to weaken. You will be better placed to assess opportunities calmly, with your own reasoning behind the decision.

#9835. AttackIQ Research Reveals How Iranian Cyber Groups Hand Off Network Access to Enable Destructive Attacks

Analysis of 20 Iranian state-sponsored threat groups details how espionage, ransomware, and hacktivism intersect in state-backed cyber campaigns.

ANTA CLARA, Calif. — (BUSINESS WIRE) — AttackIQ, the leader in threat-informed Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM), today released new research that connects previously fragmented reporting on individual Iranian cyber campaigns to map the relationships among state-sponsored operators and the institutions supporting them. The findings show Iranian espionage groups turn compromised networks into launchpads for other operators, transforming intelligence-gathering operations into destructive attacks.

Threat reporting on Iran typically covers one campaign at a time, and vendors track the same groups under different names. Helix Kitten alone appears under eight other names, including OilRig, APT34 and Scarred Manticore. AttackIQ’s Adversary Research Team consolidated that reporting into Weighing Cyber Power: Evaluating the Strategic and Operational Significance of Iran’s State-Sponsored Cyber Capability, a single map of 20 Iranian adversaries, the government institutions they are linked to and the contractors that supply their personnel, tooling and infrastructure.

Related:Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

“The value of threat research is measured by the decisions it informs,” said Paul Reid, VP of Adversary Research at AttackIQ. “Understanding which Iranian groups work together, and how confident we can be in each relationship, gives defenders a clear starting point for emulation and a realistic picture of what could follow an initial compromise. It turns a single detection into a forecast of what comes next.”

The report traces how a single intrusion can pass between groups. In one documented case, Helix Kitten (Scarred Manticore), conducted prolonged intelligence collection inside a network before handing off the network access to Banished Kitten (Void Manticore), which pursued destructive objectives. In a second case, Static Kitten (Mango Sandstorm) established access and passed it to Storm-1084, a destructive operator. In a separate campaign against the Albanian government, four separately tracked groups contributed to the same operation, which spanned reconnaissance, initial access, data theft and the deployment of destructive tooling.

When the damage arrives, it is frequently disguised. The research also found Iranian groups staging destructive attacks as ransomware or hacktivism, obscuring the intent behind the attacks. Pioneer Kitten provided criminal ransomware affiliates with access to compromised networks.

The organizations hit first may be a route to other targets. Several groups can gain access to more heavily defended organizations, including in the defense industrial base, through their subsidiaries, contractors, and suppliers.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

The analysis classifies 20 Iranian adversaries into three weight classes based on their organizational significance, operational relevance, and demonstrated capabilities. The classifications underscore that even smaller, specialized groups can play critical roles in larger cyber campaigns.

Heavyweight: Established groups with sustained espionage operations, internally developed tooling and a central role in Iran’s cyber strategy.

Lightweight: Groups with more focused missions, including specialized espionage, access facilitation and destructive operations.

Featherweight: Groups with narrower or less consistently documented activity, some relying on support from more established adversaries.

“Iran isn’t as technically sophisticated as China, Russia or North Korea, but what it lacks in sophistication it makes up for in cadence,” said Francis Guibernau, Senior Adversary Research Engineer at AttackIQ. “They target anything and everything, on every operating system and in industrial environments. That volume, combined with how freely these groups share access, is what makes the ecosystem dangerous.”

Related:Shadowy AI Relay Disables OpenAI Codex, Claude Code Sandboxes

The research draws on more than 200 references and consolidates more than 2,600 procedures, 1,300 file indicators, and 2,300 network indicators. The analysis was also validated against threat intelligence and real-world activity observed by several Fortune 150 companies actively targeted by Iranian threat actors. The research team also received input from National Computer Incident Response Teams (CIRTs) and members of the intelligence community.

To help organizations put the research into practice, AttackIQ will be releasing adversary emulations based on the documented tactics, techniques, and procedures of Iranian threat actors over the coming weeks. These emulations will enable security teams to safely test their defenses against relevant adversary behaviors, identify gaps in detection and prevention, and prioritize improvements based on real-world threat intelligence.

For a closer look at the findings with AttackIQ’s adversary research team, join the December 10 webinar, Breaking Down Iran’s Most Dangerous Cyber Tactics.

AttackIQ is the leader in threat-informed Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM), helping organizations continuously validate defenses, break attack paths, and reduce threat debt through evidence-based security operations.

Through AVA Agentic OS, AttackIQ has introduced the industry’s first agentic operating system purpose-built for CTEM, enabling organizations to execute Continuous Threat Exposure Management autonomously at enterprise scale.

By orchestrating specialized AI agents across threat intelligence, adversary exposure validation, security validation, detection engineering, control optimization, threat debt reduction, and AI security validation, AttackIQ transforms fragmented security activities into continuous cyber resilience.

Trusted by the world’s largest enterprises, government agencies, and managed security providers, AttackIQ empowers organizations to continuously discover, validate, and reduce cyber risk with confidence.

#9834. How AI Is Changing the Way Companies Hire, Manage and Measure Performance

Dmitry Kushnikov joined Manychat as its first employee in 2016, became CTO and later COO, and today holds both roles. As the company grew to more than 400 people in 24 countries, he was at the center of each major change in how it works: he designed and then led the 2018 move to cross-functional teams under Large-Scale Scrum, has run the company’s OKR system since 2020, and, as COO and CTO, now leads its AI transformation. In this interview, he discusses how AI is reshaping hiring, productivity, and the role of managers.

You joined Manychat as its first employee in 2016 and went on to become CTO and COO, being critical in scaling the company to more than 400 employees. How has that experience shaped your approach to hiring and organizational growth, and how are AI agents changing the decisions you make about expanding teams?

It taught me that every stage needs a different company, not just a bigger one. Until autumn 2017 we all worked from home, with almost no system. Then we got an office, and in 2018 we moved to cross-functional teams. In 2020 COVID sent everyone home again, and later we came back as a hybrid company. In 2022 and 2023 we went from one city to a global company with several hubs. Each time, the way we worked had to change before the headcount did.

Every new role is a cost, and not only a financial one: it also costs everyone’s time. So before opening a role, the question is whether the work should exist at all, and whether it can be done differently: start, stop, continue, or automate. AI agents make the last option real for much more of the work, so the bar for opening a role is higher than it was.

In 2018, you led Manychat's transition from functional departments to cross-functional teams using Large-Scale Scrum, an experience you later shared at TeamLead Conf in 2020 and the LeSS Conference in 2024. What problem did this transformation solve, and why do you believe the model now needs to evolve for the AI era?

The problem was accountability. In our early years we worked in functional teams: backend, frontend, design, each doing its part. When something went wrong, it wasn’t clear who owned the result, and responsibility moved from one team to another. I optimize at the team level. A team should be able to act as an independent unit that nothing can stop from reaching its result. Then it’s clear what to hold it accountable for.

So in June 2018, at about 30 people, we decided to test Large-Scale Scrum and move to cross-functional teams, each owning a customer problem end to end. Later we grouped teams into product areas and built communities of practice, so engineers in different teams still share standards. I spoke about how this worked for us at TeamLead Conf in 2020 and at the LeSS Conference in 2024.

The idea we kept is that how work is organized is separate from who reports to whom. Our Product Group is a virtual organization, and our AI Lab is built the same way.

Now we’re rethinking it again. Most agile frameworks teach that less is more, and with AI agents a small team can now do far more than it could even two years ago. That changes how product and engineering should work together, and what worked in 2018 won’t fit as it is. We’re working on it, and we’d rather talk about it once it proves itself.

As a member of Manychat's executive team, you developed The Manychat Way, a set of ten operating principles published in 2026. How have these principles influenced management decisions, particularly the decision not to measure employees by their use of AI tools?

They change decisions more than they change what we believe. Nothing in The Manychat Way was invented in 2026. We’ve had five values for years, and the ten principles are their heritage and their interpretation: how those values work when a decision is hard. We wrote them as an executive team, starting from more than twenty drafts at an offsite in February, and published them in May.

The part that changes decisions is that each principle names what we’re willing to sacrifice for it. “We prioritize ruthlessly” comes with “let some fires burn.” That gives a manager the words to stop a decent project and put the team on a great one.

It has already made at least one company-wide call. When many companies started pushing people to use LLMs more and counting the usage, we went the other way: we don’t count it. We celebrate outcomes, not outputs, so LLM usage and tokens will never be a number we ask people to hit.

Having overseen technology and operations at Manychat as the company expanded, you've had to establish ways of measuring performance across a growing organization. How do you distinguish genuine productivity from activity, especially as employees adopt AI tools?

Productivity is about the value a team creates; the process is secondary. So we agree on the result before the work starts: every objective needs a clear answer to “how will we know we achieved it?”, and key results have to be obvious and measurable.

Then we’re careful with anything that’s easy to count. Goodhart’s law applies here: the moment a measure becomes the target, it stops measuring anything real. When we started our AI transformation, managers asked whether we would measure each person’s use of AI tools. We won’t, and I don’t remember us ever counting lines of code either.

Two more rules. We commit people only to what they can actually control. The big outcome numbers live at the level of the whole company, because when every team optimizes its own number, the system breaks. And we don’t celebrate output. It works like Tetris: a filled line disappears, and the bar resets.

You’ve led engineering teams at Manychat since its early years, eventually becoming CTO and COO. How has your approach to hiring senior technical talent evolved, and why do you believe the expectations for a senior engineer in 2027 will differ from those in 2024?

Five years ago I wrote to the whole company that recruitment, usually head-hunting, was the most important of my tasks, and that was literally true. Today recruiting has its own team and leaders. The belief behind it hasn’t changed: the main skill of a leader is hiring people, ideally stronger than yourself.

What changed is the bar. For senior roles we look for validated and reflected experience: enough time in one place to live through the consequences of your own decisions and learn from them. With people from big companies, the question is what luggage they bring and what they will leave outside. And before we hire a senior person, we have to be able to say clearly what they will own in their first six months. If we can’t, the interview isn’t fair to the candidate.

The AI era is moving the bar again. A senior engineer of 2027 works with AI agents as partners, and that is a completely different way of thinking: you have to choose it. The job moves from writing every line to owning the result end to end, from what should be built to whether it works. That takes product judgment: I don’t believe an engineer without a vision of the product can do it well. We’re still writing the new criteria down, but that’s the direction.

Customer support became part of your scope at the end of 2023, and AI agents now handle its first line. What prompted this shift, and what results have you seen?

At the end of 2023 customer support became part of my scope, and I became the executive overseeing it. In early 2024 it was the first place where our growth hit hard: tickets grew faster than the team could handle, and for a while people across the company were answering them.

My role was strategic: shaping where support should go given what was happening in the company, and setting the direction. In 2025 that direction was that the first line goes to an AI agent. Our Head of Customer Experience and the CX team built the operation: they chose the tool against their own test thresholds and rolled it out to all customers.

We also measure it in a way that’s fair to the team. The team is accountable for the quality of its own service, and we track separately the complaints that come from product issues or third-party platforms.

Monthly ticket volume is about twice what it was in early 2024, and customer satisfaction rose from about 84% at the start of 2024 to about 90% through 2025.

Manychat operates across 24 countries and 16 hours of time zones. As the executive responsible for technology strategy and the AI Lab, how have you approached AI adoption across this distributed organization? What measurable results have you achieved so far?

We treat AI adoption as pull, not push. Most of the real practice started with a handful of people in different teams and countries who found what works and shared it openly, and our job is to make it easy for that to spread. In sensitive areas like security, payments and data access, we keep a person in the loop.

We measure outcomes, not usage. Support is where we measured first: the measure is the cost to serve a resolved conversation, paired with customer satisfaction. Since the end of 2024 ticket volume has roughly doubled, while the frontline team grew by about a third.

Outside support we’re still finding the right measure for each function, and until we have one we’d rather not count activity.

After a decade building Manychat, you've described the manager of the future as a "visionary operator." How do you expect AI to transform management and organizational structures over the next three to five years, and how are you preparing Manychat for those changes?

Managers’ work will change the most. AI agents will take over more of the routine, and what stays with people is judgment, vision and responsibility for other people. The profile we want to grow is the visionary operator: someone who can see where we’re going and also make it happen. AI agents help close the gaps on both sides. They complement people; they don’t replace them.

The way we prepare starts with one position: if you want to lead a transformation, start with yourself, not with cutting your people. A company only changes when each of us does, so leaders go first; I worked it through on myself before asking anyone else to.

Then we give everyone access to the tools, with budgets and licenses for the whole company, and we invest in training. And we’re changing how the company works with information: everything that can live as a policy or a process is written down and kept in a repository, so people and AI agents work from the same source.

You've risen from Manychat's first employee to CTO and COO, helping build an international technology company. What advice would you give to other engineers and technology leaders who aspire to achieve similar success?

Work on self-awareness before anything else. It’s a general leadership skill more than a people-management one: you can’t help your team until you understand where you are yourself, and people copy behavior, not instructions.

Then expect the bar to keep moving. When a company grows as fast as ours, staying at the same level means falling behind: you need to exceed to meet. Every stage asked for something I hadn’t done before, and the hardest part was usually letting go of what I was best at.
